name: Molly Gray
subject: Happy back to school, Vermont!
body:
Dear Peter, This week, students across Vermont are heading back to school, and I want to wish every one of them a wonderful year ahead. To all the kids: _be curious, be kind, ask questions, make new friends, and never stop learning. Every day is a new opportunity to grow and learn._ And to Vermont’s teachers, educators, and school staff: _thank you. Your dedication, patience, and care make a difference in the lives of our children and communities every single day. We see you, we appreciate you, and we’re grateful for all that you do._ I’m proud to be a product of Vermont’s education system. I know firsthand how essential our schools are. Not just to our children, but to the strength of our communities, especially in rural Vermont. Vermont’s schools are facing real challenges. As Lt. Governor, I’ll support giving communities a voice in education reform, including voluntary mergers, shared services, and other locally led solutions. I’ll work to restart Vermont’s School Construction Trust Fund so every community can afford safe, modern schools, and I’ll push to address rising healthcare costs, one of the biggest drivers of school budgets and property taxes. Today, I hope you’ll join me in thanking a teacher, parent, paraeducator, custodian, principal, or school staff member for everything they do for our kids and communities. Here’s to a great school year!

* * *
[](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/137977374/642566759/-261618493?refcode=AU_MKH_FR_TAN_GEN_AC_20260826_PM1_V1_S1&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMDUvMS83MTU3NCIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICI2NjEwZWU1Yi04MWExLWYxMTEtOWIzMy0wMDIyNDgyYTlmMWQiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=9VfOWj93_J6W27ULTKG0yfYCrN0Tlm-GXcl6H0w8lI8=) Peter — My name is Mary Peltola, and after winning our open primary, I am officially running in the general election for United States Senate in Alaska. I want to share with you why I made the decision to run – and to ask for your support as we begin the general election together. But if you already understand how important this race and your support are, and you’re ready to join our fight for fish, family, and freedom, please use this button to split a contribution between my campaign for U.S. Senate and Mazie Hirono: | [CONTRIBUTE](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/137977375/642566760/-261618493?refcode=AU_MKH_FR_TAN_GEN_AC_20260826_PM1_V1_S1&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMDUvMS83MTU3NCIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICI2NjEwZWU1Yi04MWExLWYxMTEtOWIzMy0wMDIyNDgyYTlmMWQiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=9VfOWj93_J6W27ULTKG0yfYCrN0Tlm-GXcl6H0w8lI8=)

Now here’s a bit more on how I came to this decision.
When I was growing up in Bethel, salmon fishing with my father in the summers and dog mushing in the winters, Alaska was a place of abundance.
Now, all across Alaska, we have scarcity.
Multi-national companies are trawling our waters and decimating our fish stocks. The moose, caribou, and migratory birds that used to fill our freezers are harder to find.
So we buy more groceries, where the prices are just crushing Alaska families.
And I've got to tell you, DC people do not care that we are paying nearly 20 bucks for a gallon of fuel. They don’t even believe us.
They're focused on their own wallets – not ours.
And when they actually work together on something, it’s usually to help themselves. The rigged system in DC is shutting down Alaska and hurting all of us while politicians and their millionaire and billionaire donors feather their own nest.
It’s why our prices keep rising, all while the healthcare and services Alaskans rely on get gutted.
I'm done with politicians getting richer while things get tougher here at home.
My agenda for Alaska will always be: fish, family, freedom. These values have been the core values of my campaigns since the very beginning.
But if we’re going to secure Alaska’s future, we need another priority: fighting corruption.
I'm running for Alaska's Senate seat because it is the fight for our future.
**This is going to be the closest and most consequential Senate race this year, and I cannot do this alone. There is only one way we’ll be able to flip this seat... and that is together.**
So I am asking:
**[Please split a contribution between Mazie Hirono and my campaign for the U.S. Senate today before our end-of-month deadline. We are looking for a huge surge in support to get our general election campaign off to a strong start and put us in a position to win. No donation is too small. Multi-national companies are trawling our waters and decimating our fish stocks. The moose, caribou, and migratory birds that used to fill our freezers are harder to find. # [They Lost the Right to Keep Inspectors Out. So Now ICE Wants to Own the Building.](https://substack.com/app-link/post?publication_id=3260111&post_id=212890377&utm_source=post-email-title&utm_campaign=email-post-title&isFreemail=true&r=1hvr60&token=eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjo5MDUwMTE5MiwicG9zdF9pZCI6MjEyODkwMzc3LCJpYXQiOjE3ODc3NzEzOTAsImV4cCI6MTc5MDM2MzM5MCwiaXNzIjoicHViLTMyNjAxMTEiLCJzdWIiOiJwb3N0LXJlYWN0aW9uIn0.P9PCMlu07kdAHm9rpW0rc2dk8-fk76h9DNB8wDtPv_U)
### What a possible sale of Tacoma's ICE detention center teaches us about the difference between winning a lawsuit and actually winning oversight.

---

**Last year, my husband survived 124 days captive inside the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma.**
Zahid is a 100-percent disabled American military veteran. He's been here almost 30 years - always came here legally - served in the military with honor - and has **never** broken any US laws. He doesn't have so much as a parking ticket. His family's been here since the 1980s, as scientists, doctors, professors, and researchers, whose work has benefited the US and all of humanity. Neighbors rely on him. Friends turn to him for counsel when in crisis. He's a peaceful, principled, upstanding pillar of the community, and has been for decades.
Bottom line: **he never should have been there in the first place.** And get this - he was abducted from a citizenship appointment.
We fought his illegal detention across four federal jurisdictions without a lawyer, because we could not afford one and because the machinery of federal detention does not become easier to navigate merely because the government is wrong. On December 22, 2025, a federal judge ordered his immediate release, calling his detention "flat out wrong."
**[We won.](https://substack.com/redirect/10923a45-1172-4984-b478-e83537a3534e?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** That sentence is true... and so is everything the word _won_ leaves out.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/7a8834c3-071a-481f-9095-6782a7c095be?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Muhammad Zahid Chaudhry, US Army, Retired, holding our sleeping son. January 2026, less than a month after his release from illegal ICE detention.
**I know that facility.** I know the particular smell of the lobby, some combination of sterile and neglected. I know the magazine shelf whose magazines do not seem to change. I know the tactile sensation of walking through the gate in the chain-link fence, topped with multiple strands of barbed wire, passing the guardhouse and following the walkway alongside a perfectly ordinary employee parking lot, complete with designated "Employee of the Month" spaces and a striking number of expensive vehicles. I know what it feels like to be walking voluntarily into a place your husband cannot voluntarily leave.
What stays with me most is the **terrible ordinariness of it**. The people who control whether I am allowed to see my husband do not know how to pronounce his name and often do not seem particularly concerned about learning. They talk with one another about weekend barbecues or the latest WWE fight. They clock in, and out. They get paid well to be there. They have coworkers and parking spaces and lunch breaks and plans for Saturday. And I stand at the desk asking permission to see my husband--the soul of my soul, the light of my life--as though the most important human being in my world were a package being processed through somebody else's workplace.
I know the high-school-style lockers where visitors leave their belongings. I know the bare white cinderblock walls. I know the obscene little geography of the lobby, where a room called a "court" sits right next door to the visitor hall, as though justice and imprisonment were merely neighboring administrative functions. I know the tiny metal visiting cubicles, stainless steel counters, small white walls covered in scrawling pleas and outrage, where you pick up a corded telephone with the tinny speakers and converse with someone you love who has been convicted of no crime, who has done nothing wrong, and whom you are nevertheless forbidden to touch. We put our hands up to the glass anyway. When I brought the children, Zahid would smile, make funny faces, and tap his wedding ring on the glass to keep their attention - the only forms of a father's loving play that he was able to give them.
And I know what comes through that telephone, leaking past the attempts to keep smiling for my sake. Communications outages. Terrible food. Abusive guards. Suicide attempts and mental-health crises. Medical care so inadequate that people learn to stop expecting it. Legal access that would be laughable if the consequences were not so serious. Dirty facilities. Loud televisions broadcasting violent programming into spaces where there is nowhere else to go. Bright, inescapable florescent lights you cannot control that dim only partially, from roughly midnight until five in the morning, and otherwise remain on. A breakfast that can amount to half a cup of cornflakes and a small scoop of the previous night's mashed potatoes. The daily accumulation of small indignities that sound almost petty when you write them down individually and become something very different when a human being has no power to escape any of them.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/00873a5e-d9df-44d5-83b1-7bfe960c80d0?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Muhammad Zahid Chaudhry, US Army, Retired. Decorated, 100% disabled, wheelchair bound, American soldier. **Illegally detained by ICE.**
Then the visit ends, and this is the part that nearly broke me every time: **I get to leave.**
I walk back down the same path, through the same gate and past the same guardhouse, and suddenly the world is enormous again. I can feel air moving across my face. I can look up and see clouds. Throughout those 124 days, I watched the row of trees outside the facility slowly change color, then shed their leaves. The weather moved from hot to warm to cool to crisp. The angle of the sunlight changed. Some days the sky was brilliant; some days the clouds were layered and gray; some days the wind had that unmistakable sharpness that means autumn has arrived. I noticed all of it with an almost painful intensity because I knew Zahid could not. Seasons were happening to the world, and my husband was being kept apart from them.
> That building taught me how much of freedom consists of things we barely notice until someone takes them away: **weather, darkness, silence, the smell of leaves, sleeping the night through, choosing what to eat, calling your doctor, opening a door, walking outside, touching the person you love.**
[ Share](https://substack.com/app-link/post?publication_id=3260111&post_id=212890377&utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&utm_campaign=email-share&action=share&triggerShare=true&isFreemail=true&r=1hvr60&token=eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjo5MDUwMTE5MiwicG9zdF9pZCI6MjEyODkwMzc3LCJpYXQiOjE3ODc3NzEzOTAsImV4cCI6MTc5MDM2MzM5MCwiaXNzIjoicHViLTMyNjAxMTEiLCJzdWIiOiJwb3N0LXJlYWN0aW9uIn0.P9PCMlu07kdAHm9rpW0rc2dk8-fk76h9DNB8wDtPv_U)
**So I want to be very clear about the moral premise from which I am writing this.** The Northwest ICE Processing Center, and facilities like it, are a stain on this country, a stain on my state, and a stain on our conscience. They are not some foreign cruelty accidentally imported into American life. This is a homegrown American abomination, built through American law, American contracts, American corporations, American tax dollars and American political choices. It must be resisted, and ultimately it must end.
In the meantime, human beings are still inside it. Which means who is allowed to see what happens behind those walls matters enormously.
**And that brings us to what ICE and GEO Group appear to be doing now.**
GEO Group, the private, **for-profit** prison corporation that has operated NWIPC for years, **is negotiating the sale of detention facilities to ICE itself.** In July, ICE sought a turnkey detention facility within 30 miles of its Tukwila office, with at least 1,500 beds. NWIPC is inside that radius. It has 1,575 beds. GEO has told investors that it is negotiating sales of multiple facilities to ICE and hopes to settle pricing by the end of September. ICE has declined to say publicly that the Tacoma facility is the one it intends to buy, but the specifications leave remarkably little mystery about the possibility.
The deal GEO has described would not mean GEO goes away. Quite the opposite. Under the structure presented to investors, ICE would purchase the property and GEO would continue operating it under a long-term management contract. GEO gets the capital payout from selling the asset. GEO keeps the operating revenue from running the detention center. The people behind the glass remain under substantially the same private management. The meaningful change is who owns the building.
That may sound like unimportant paperwork. It is not.
**The deed is where the next legal strategy begins.**
GEO founder George Zoley has publicly described federal ownership as a way around state oversight. ICE's acquisition paperwork for the Seattle-area facility reportedly invokes "federal supremacy": the theory that federal ownership and federal control strengthen the government's ability to put detention operations beyond the reach of state and local laws. **Insulation from state authority is one of the advantages of federal ownership that the people pursuing this model have** _**themselves**_**described.**
[ Upgrade to paid](https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9tZWxpc3NhNGNvbmdyZXNzLnN1YnN0YWNrLmNvbS9zdWJzY3JpYmU_.6YYfRJ8QOii3mDksv6pMcutxo4BFIYF1dc1eYXXL_UA?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget&utm_content=212890377)
To understand why they would care so much about that advantage right now, you have to understand what Washington State just spent **three years** fighting to establish.
In 2023, Washington enacted HB 1470 and HB 1232, creating health, sanitation, food, medical-care and inspection requirements for private detention facilities. The underlying proposition was almost painfully modest: **if human beings are confined inside a privately operated detention center in Washington, state authorities ought to be able to verify that they are being housed safely, fed adequately, treated medically, and kept under conditions consistent with basic public-health standards.
**
**GEO fought to keep inspectors outside anyway.** Its argument was essentially that because it was performing detention work for the federal government, Washington could not regulate it as an ordinary private company. In August 2025, the Ninth Circuit rejected the heart of that claim. A private corporation does not become the sovereign merely because the sovereign hires it. Doing federal work does not transform GEO Group into the United States government.
The inspection mandate took effect in March 2026, and GEO continued refusing entry. Washington officials documented ten attempted inspections and more than 3,500 complaints. Finally, on July 9, U.S. District Judge Benjamin Settle ordered GEO to admit Washington Department of Health inspectors, while carving out certain administrative and medical areas controlled directly by ICE.
Consider the sequence.
-> Washington spends years establishing its authority to inspect.
-> GEO spends years fighting that authority.
-> GEO loses.
-> A federal judge finally orders the company to open the doors.
-> Within weeks, ICE seeks to purchase a **privately** owned detention facility whose location and capacity fit NWIPC almost perfectly.
-> Soon afterward, GEO confirms that it is negotiating facility sales to ICE, while its own leadership has already **described** federal ownership as a means of escaping state oversight.
They lost the argument that a private contractor should be treated as though it were the federal government. Now the federal government may buy the building and give them a stronger version of the same argument.
That is the move.
_It is also not necessarily as legally decisive as ICE and GEO would like it to be._
[ Share](https://substack.com/app-link/post?publication_id=3260111&post_id=212890377&utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&utm_campaign=email-share&action=share&triggerShare=true&isFreemail=true&r=1hvr60&token=eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjo5MDUwMTE5MiwicG9zdF9pZCI6MjEyODkwMzc3LCJpYXQiOjE3ODc3NzEzOTAsImV4cCI6MTc5MDM2MzM5MCwiaXNzIjoicHViLTMyNjAxMTEiLCJzdWIiOiJwb3N0LXJlYWN0aW9uIn0.P9PCMlu07kdAHm9rpW0rc2dk8-fk76h9DNB8wDtPv_U)
Washington law does not define a "private detention facility" according to who owns the real estate. It defines one according to who operates it. The statute applies to facilities "operated by a private, nongovernmental entity" under a government contract. If ICE owns NWIPC while GEO continues running it under contract, GEO remains a private corporation operating a detention center. Washington's Department of Health has already made this point publicly, noting that NWIPC "does not sit on a federal enclave, so state laws still apply."
Here's what that means: **Federal ownership of land is not the same thing as exclusive federal jurisdiction over land**. The United States owns buildings and property all over the country without turning every parcel into territory beyond state authority. A federal enclave involves a distinct constitutional and jurisdictional status. ICE cannot simply purchase a building in Pierce County and thereby transform NWIPC into the legal equivalent of Joint Base Lewis-McChord.
Buying the building gives them a stronger argument. It does not necessarily give them the whole argument.
**But the deed itself is not the part that concerns me most.**
Judge Settle's July order has already shown us exactly where the more dangerous fight may occur. The court drew a boundary _inside the facility_ : areas operated by GEO that Washington may inspect, and certain administrative and medical areas controlled directly by ICE that state inspectors may not enter. Once that distinction exists, the fight can stop being about whether Washington has authority over "the detention center" and become a much more granular fight over who controls each room, each function, each service, each record and each decision.
**That opens the door to a form of erosion that is much harder for the public to see.** A medical function becomes more directly federal. An administrative responsibility moves under ICE control. Contract language changes. One area is reclassified, then another. The operator says, _not this room_. ICE says, _not this function_. Another small piece of the institution disappears behind the shield of federal control.
Nobody ever has to announce that oversight has been abolished. Nobody has to win a dramatic Supreme Court case declaring Washington powerless. The portion of the facility available to meaningful outside inspection can simply become smaller and smaller until the state retains authority in theory while losing the practical ability to see enough of the institution to exercise it.
I know why that matters, because I know how difficult it already is to know what happens inside.
When Zahid told me about the food, I could not walk into the kitchen and look. When he told me about medical neglect, I could not walk into the clinic and ask questions. When communications went down, the very mechanism by which I might learn what was happening disappeared with them. When people experienced mental-health crises, when someone attempted suicide, when guards behaved abusively, when conditions were filthy or lights never properly went dark, **the people experiencing those things were also the people with the** _**least**_**ability to document them, leave them, or compel anyone outside to care.**
### That is what inspection is for.
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9tZWxpc3NhNGNvbmdyZXNzLnN1YnN0YWNrLmNvbS9zdWJzY3JpYmU_.6YYfRJ8QOii3mDksv6pMcutxo4BFIYF1dc1eYXXL_UA?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget&utm_content=212890377)
And my husband's case taught me something else about systems like this: whenever responsibility approaches, authority has an extraordinary ability to fragment. GEO can say ICE makes the rules. ICE can say GEO operates the facility. Medical care belongs to one chain of authority, custody to another, immigration adjudication to another, transportation to another. Each institution can possess tremendous power over a human being while disclaiming responsibility for the whole of what is happening to them.
The human being remains trapped inside, anyway. Subjected to all of it.
A system capable of moving authority around faster than accountability can follow it is not meaningful oversight. It is a liability shield around something remarkably akin to an administrative torture chamber.
**Congress could make this maneuver much harder.** Federal law could state plainly that state health and safety protections remain applicable to privately operated detention facilities regardless of who owns the underlying property, subject only to narrow limits genuinely necessary for federal functions. Congress could demand the proposed sale agreement before it closes. Members could subpoena the operating contract. They could ask which functions ICE intends to designate as directly federal, which portions of the facility state inspectors would consequently lose access to, and exactly what legal authority ICE believes allows that result.
Those are not especially complicated questions. The difficult part is forcing powerful institutions to answer them _before_ a transaction closes and a new arrangement hardens into ordinary practice.
That is what **oversight** is supposed to do.
This is also why I care so much about doing independent work in public now. Procurement documents are boring. Corporate filings are dense. Jurisdictional arguments are easy to bury beneath acronyms and procedural language. Private prison corporations are sophisticated political actors, and federal agencies know how to defend their authority. Systems like this benefit enormously from the assumption that eventually everyone outside them will become exhausted, distracted or bored.
I am none of those things.
The deed matters. The operating agreement matters more. Who controls the medical unit matters. Who employs the guards matters. Who owns the records matters. Who decides which door an inspector may walk through matters. And it matters whether somebody is still reading the documents after the acquisition announcement falls out of the news cycle.
I will be.
I'll be watching the procurement records, GEO's disclosures, the Pierce County property filings, the operating agreement and any attempt to move another piece of this facility beyond public scrutiny. If NWIPC changes hands, I want to know precisely what changes with it--and precisely what does not.
My family already learned what happens when a human being disappears behind those walls and accountability cannot reach him.
The next family should not have to learn it the same way.
**Care. Courage. The Constitution.**

What a possible sale of Tacoma's ICE detention center teaches us about the difference between winning a lawsuit and actually winning oversight. | | | Aug 26 | | | | | | | | | | | | Last year, my husband survived 124 days captive inside the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma. Zahid is a 100-percent disabled American military veteran. He's been here almost 30 years - always came here legally - served in the military with honor - and has never broken any US laws. He doesn't have so much as a parking ticket. His family's been here since the 1980s, as scientists, doctors, professors, and researchers, whose work has benefited the US and all of humanity. Neighbors rely on him. Friends turn to him for counsel when in crisis. He's a peaceful, principled, upstanding pillar of the community, and has been for decades. Bottom line: he never should have been there in the first place. And get this - he was abducted from a citizenship appointment. We fought his illegal detention across four federal jurisdictions without a lawyer, because we could not afford one and because the machinery of federal detention does not become easier to navigate merely because the government is wrong. On December 22, 2025, a federal judge ordered his immediate release, calling his detention "flat out wrong." That sentence is true... and so is everything the word won leaves out. | | ---|---|--- Muhammad Zahid Chaudhry, US Army, Retired, holding our sleeping son. January 2026, less than a month after his release from illegal ICE detention. I know that facility. I know the particular smell of the lobby, some combination of sterile and neglected. I know the magazine shelf whose magazines do not seem to change. I know the tactile sensation of walking through the gate in the chain-link fence, topped with multiple strands of barbed wire, passing the guardhouse and following the walkway alongside a perfectly ordinary employee parking lot, complete with designated "Employee of the Month" spaces and a striking number of expensive vehicles. I know what it feels like to be walking voluntarily into a place your husband cannot voluntarily leave. What stays with me most is the terrible ordinariness of it. The people who control whether I am allowed to see my husband do not know how to pronounce his name and often do not seem particularly concerned about learning. They talk with one another about weekend barbecues or the latest WWE fight. They clock in, and out. They get paid well to be there. They have coworkers and parking spaces and lunch breaks and plans for Saturday. And I stand at the desk asking permission to see my husband--the soul of my soul, the light of my life--as though the most important human being in my world were a package being processed through somebody else's workplace. I know the high-school-style lockers where visitors leave their belongings. I know the bare white cinderblock walls. I know the obscene little geography of the lobby, where a room called a "court" sits right next door to the visitor hall, as though justice and imprisonment were merely neighboring administrative functions. I know the tiny metal visiting cubicles, stainless steel counters, small white walls covered in scrawling pleas and outrage, where you pick up a corded telephone with the tinny speakers and converse with someone you love who has been convicted of no crime, who has done nothing wrong, and whom you are nevertheless forbidden to touch. We put our hands up to the glass anyway. When I brought the children, Zahid would smile, make funny faces, and tap his wedding ring on the glass to keep their attention - the only forms of a father's loving play that he was able to give them. And I know what comes through that telephone, leaking past the attempts to keep smiling for my sake. Communications outages. Terrible food. Abusive guards. Suicide attempts and mental-health crises. Medical care so inadequate that people learn to stop expecting it. Legal access that would be laughable if the consequences were not so serious. Dirty facilities. Loud televisions broadcasting violent programming into spaces where there is nowhere else to go. Bright, inescapable florescent lights you cannot control that dim only partially, from roughly midnight until five in the morning, and otherwise remain on. A breakfast that can amount to half a cup of cornflakes and a small scoop of the previous night's mashed potatoes. The daily accumulation of small indignities that sound almost petty when you write them down individually and become something very different when a human being has no power to escape any of them. | | ---|---|--- Muhammad Zahid Chaudhry, US Army, Retired. Decorated, 100% disabled, wheelchair bound, American soldier. Illegally detained by ICE. Then the visit ends, and this is the part that nearly broke me every time: I get to leave. I walk back down the same path, through the same gate and past the same guardhouse, and suddenly the world is enormous again. I can feel air moving across my face. I can look up and see clouds. Throughout those 124 days, I watched the row of trees outside the facility slowly change color, then shed their leaves. The weather moved from hot to warm to cool to crisp. The angle of the sunlight changed. Some days the sky was brilliant; some days the clouds were layered and gray; some days the wind had that unmistakable sharpness that means autumn has arrived. I noticed all of it with an almost painful intensity because I knew Zahid could not. Seasons were happening to the world, and my husband was being kept apart from them. That building taught me how much of freedom consists of things we barely notice until someone takes them away: weather, darkness, silence, the smell of leaves, sleeping the night through, choosing what to eat, calling your doctor, opening a door, walking outside, touching the person you love. So I want to be very clear about the moral premise from which I am writing this. The Northwest ICE Processing Center, and facilities like it, are a stain on this country, a stain on my state, and a stain on our conscience. They are not some foreign cruelty accidentally imported into American life. This is a homegrown American abomination, built through American law, American contracts, American corporations, American tax dollars and American political choices. It must be resisted, and ultimately it must end. In the meantime, human beings are still inside it. Which means who is allowed to see what happens behind those walls matters enormously. And that brings us to what ICE and GEO Group appear to be doing now. GEO Group, the private, for-profit prison corporation that has operated NWIPC for years, is negotiating the sale of detention facilities to ICE itself. In July, ICE sought a turnkey detention facility within 30 miles of its Tukwila office, with at least 1,500 beds. NWIPC is inside that radius. It has 1,575 beds. GEO has told investors that it is negotiating sales of multiple facilities to ICE and hopes to settle pricing by the end of September. ICE has declined to say publicly that the Tacoma facility is the one it intends to buy, but the specifications leave remarkably little mystery about the possibility. The deal GEO has described would not mean GEO goes away. Quite the opposite. Under the structure presented to investors, ICE would purchase the property and GEO would continue operating it under a long-term management contract. GEO gets the capital payout from selling the asset. GEO keeps the operating revenue from running the detention center. The people behind the glass remain under substantially the same private management. The meaningful change is who owns the building. That may sound like unimportant paperwork. It is not. The deed is where the next legal strategy begins. GEO founder George Zoley has publicly described federal ownership as a way around state oversight. ICE's acquisition paperwork for the Seattle-area facility reportedly invokes "federal supremacy": the theory that federal ownership and federal control strengthen the government's ability to put detention operations beyond the reach of state and local laws. Insulation from state authority is one of the advantages of federal ownership that the people pursuing this model have themselvesdescribed. To understand why they would care so much about that advantage right now, you have to understand what Washington State just spent three years fighting to establish. In 2023, Washington enacted HB 1470 and HB 1232, creating health, sanitation, food, medical-care and inspection requirements for private detention facilities. The underlying proposition was almost painfully modest: if human beings are confined inside a privately operated detention center in Washington, state authorities ought to be able to verify that they are being housed safely, fed adequately, treated medically, and kept under conditions consistent with basic public-health standards. GEO fought to keep inspectors outside anyway. Its argument was essentially that because it was performing detention work for the federal government, Washington could not regulate it as an ordinary private company. In August 2025, the Ninth Circuit rejected the heart of that claim. A private corporation does not become the sovereign merely because the sovereign hires it. Doing federal work does not transform GEO Group into the United States government. The inspection mandate took effect in March 2026, and GEO continued refusing entry. Washington officials documented ten attempted inspections and more than 3,500 complaints. Finally, on July 9, U.S. District Judge Benjamin Settle ordered GEO to admit Washington Department of Health inspectors, while carving out certain administrative and medical areas controlled directly by ICE. Consider the sequence. -> Washington spends years establishing its authority to inspect. -> GEO spends years fighting that authority. -> GEO loses. -> A federal judge finally orders the company to open the doors. -> Within weeks, ICE seeks to purchase a privately owned detention facility whose location and capacity fit NWIPC almost perfectly. -> Soon afterward, GEO confirms that it is negotiating facility sales to ICE, while its own leadership has already described federal ownership as a means of escaping state oversight. They lost the argument that a private contractor should be treated as though it were the federal government. Now the federal government may buy the building and give them a stronger version of the same argument. That is the move. It is also not necessarily as legally decisive as ICE and GEO would like it to be. Washington law does not define a "private detention facility" according to who owns the real estate. It defines one according to who operates it. The statute applies to facilities "operated by a private, nongovernmental entity" under a government contract. If ICE owns NWIPC while GEO continues running it under contract, GEO remains a private corporation operating a detention center. Washington's Department of Health has already made this point publicly, noting that NWIPC "does not sit on a federal enclave, so state laws still apply." Here's what that means: Federal ownership of land is not the same thing as exclusive federal jurisdiction over land. The United States owns buildings and property all over the country without turning every parcel into territory beyond state authority. A federal enclave involves a distinct constitutional and jurisdictional status. ICE cannot simply purchase a building in Pierce County and thereby transform NWIPC into the legal equivalent of Joint Base Lewis-McChord. Buying the building gives them a stronger argument. It does not necessarily give them the whole argument. But the deed itself is not the part that concerns me most. Judge Settle's July order has already shown us exactly where the more dangerous fight may occur. The court drew a boundary inside the facility : areas operated by GEO that Washington may inspect, and certain administrative and medical areas controlled directly by ICE that state inspectors may not enter. Once that distinction exists, the fight can stop being about whether Washington has authority over "the detention center" and become a much more granular fight over who controls each room, each function, each service, each record and each decision. That opens the door to a form of erosion that is much harder for the public to see. A medical function becomes more directly federal. An administrative responsibility moves under ICE control. Contract language changes. One area is reclassified, then another. The operator says, not this room. ICE says, not this function. Another small piece of the institution disappears behind the shield of federal control. Nobody ever has to announce that oversight has been abolished. Nobody has to win a dramatic Supreme Court case declaring Washington powerless. The portion of the facility available to meaningful outside inspection can simply become smaller and smaller until the state retains authority in theory while losing the practical ability to see enough of the institution to exercise it. I know why that matters, because I know how difficult it already is to know what happens inside. When Zahid told me about the food, I could not walk into the kitchen and look. When he told me about medical neglect, I could not walk into the clinic and ask questions. When communications went down, the very mechanism by which I might learn what was happening disappeared with them. When people experienced mental-health crises, when someone attempted suicide, when guards behaved abusively, when conditions were filthy or lights never properly went dark, the people experiencing those things were also the people with the leastability to document them, leave them, or compel anyone outside to care. That is what inspection is for. And my husband's case taught me something else about systems like this: whenever responsibility approaches, authority has an extraordinary ability to fragment. GEO can say ICE makes the rules. ICE can say GEO operates the facility. Medical care belongs to one chain of authority, custody to another, immigration adjudication to another, transportation to another. Each institution can possess tremendous power over a human being while disclaiming responsibility for the whole of what is happening to them. The human being remains trapped inside, anyway. Subjected to all of it. A system capable of moving authority around faster than accountability can follow it is not meaningful oversight. It is a liability shield around something remarkably akin to an administrative torture chamber. Congress could make this maneuver much harder. Federal law could state plainly that state health and safety protections remain applicable to privately operated detention facilities regardless of who owns the underlying property, subject only to narrow limits genuinely necessary for federal functions. Congress could demand the proposed sale agreement before it closes. Members could subpoena the operating contract. They could ask which functions ICE intends to designate as directly federal, which portions of the facility state inspectors would consequently lose access to, and exactly what legal authority ICE believes allows that result. Those are not especially complicated questions. The difficult part is forcing powerful institutions to answer them before a transaction closes and a new arrangement hardens into ordinary practice. That is what oversight is supposed to do. This is also why I care so much about doing independent work in public now. Procurement documents are boring. Corporate filings are dense. Jurisdictional arguments are easy to bury beneath acronyms and procedural language. Private prison corporations are sophisticated political actors, and federal agencies know how to defend their authority. Systems like this benefit enormously from the assumption that eventually everyone outside them will become exhausted, distracted or bored. I am none of those things. The deed matters. The operating agreement matters more. Who controls the medical unit matters. Who employs the guards matters. Who owns the records matters. Who decides which door an inspector may walk through matters. And it matters whether somebody is still reading the documents after the acquisition announcement falls out of the news cycle. I will be. I'll be watching the procurement records, GEO's disclosures, the Pierce County property filings, the operating agreement and any attempt to move another piece of this facility beyond public scrutiny. If NWIPC changes hands, I want to know precisely what changes with it--and precisely what does not. My family already learned what happens when a human being disappears behind those walls and accountability cannot reach him. The next family should not have to learn it the same way. Care. Courage. The Constitution. body:
Why do we need to stop Trump's nominees?
A FedEx-linked Postmaster General already runs USPS . Add a board dominated by Trump’s corporate insider donor appointees poised to keep slowing the mail and raising prices, consolidating post offices, and outsourcing work toward privatization, and you have a recipe for disaster.
Public pressure has helped stop attacks on the USPS in the past. A federal judge just put a temporary stop on Trump turning USPS into his election administrator , blocking ballots from anyone not on a Homeland Security citizenship list. We can win here, too.

Peter,

106 years ago today, the 19th Amendment was ratified, finally recognizing women's constitutional right to vote. It was a victory generations in the making, won because women organized, marched, protested, and refused to accept a democracy where their voices didn't count.

**But that victory didn't open the ballot box equally for everyone.**

Black, Indigenous, and other women of color continued to face discriminatory laws and barriers that kept them from exercising their right to vote for decades. Even today, the fight to protect the right to vote isn't over.

MAGA Republicans continue to push new restrictions that would make voting harder for Americans to cast their ballots, with women, especially women of color and married women, among those who could face new and extreme barriers.

Peter, Kim has always believed our democracy is strongest when every eligible voter can make their voice heard. With our primary election behind us, we need to ensure we have the resources to defend that principle— _and this seat_ —all the way through November and across the finish line.

Our first end-of-month deadline since the primary is just days away, and we've set an ambitious goal to raise $60,000 before then. [1]Justice Democrats

Peter,

Just one week after he flip-flopped and declared he no longer supports
Medicare for All, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries just met privately
with Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, to discuss how they can
“cooperate.”

This is not how the leader of an opposition party should operate.

Kushner was not elected to office, nor does he hold any kind of official
government role — he’s a shameless opportunist who’s used his proximity to
the White House to make deals and develop the decimated Gaza Strip into a
luxury vacation destination for profit.

And yet, the top Democrat in Congress decided to prioritize a catch-up
with him while the Trump administration pushes us further into
authoritarianism and corruption.

This move comes at the same time Jeffries defended Islamophobic
Congressman Randy Fine, who has relentlessly attacked Rep. Ilhan Omar and
other Muslim members of Congress and introduced legislation to allow for
drivers to hit protesters with their cars.

Once again, Democratic Party leadership proves that it would rather work
with fascists than progressives.

This is yet another reminder why we must keep building our progressive
bloc in Congress and cleaning house in the Party — the more progressives
we elect, the fewer feckless, Do-Nothing Democrats there will be left in
power.

The future of the Democratic Party cannot look like leadership that
opposes widely popular and lifesaving policies like Medicare for All, but
strategizes with MAGA goons like Jared Kushner.

Hi there, I hope you are well!
[This is Michele Tafoya – I’ve got a quick story to share if you’ll indulge me for a few moments.](http://links.ourdefenseofamerica.com/u/click?_t=aa3ef0db03454a26b650c9ca7e919386&_m=3724017f04ea4c0c83c7cedd1df5854e&_e=QAhAGh1yIC7ycH1FRylgJHZ-lYOBfpHtoEsDHHNE2S4Nv8LJuLkPXdZQ0P2npep2ETDB-CWf3AdAcMc-jskLgby8WuQAWGrEFQARR1iC8T-PKDU0jt3JJE2C2dc9AJynGa06785tm9rdU8lSZuJ8G171P5pNMBIxQ8BN4gafDCeQ6-YT2SwslicwAbtep7ky554cM6OoEtQVpWt_tJSOBwK84XKKyhKWH69X07vDuQfz4SLNfPJBbfFOXzz3nDHPiZoaCNnsVDguFoguPG5_LOQM7wtQc0FcptWg7tNF1FcrkVAa5Otg4AkMvcjNVMbVpWd08vOTNH4g1Rr0OPgDYJH-lnlvcowjAaz5f1ulPPVC4N_BMY-AUK2LjVd-GcJ1AzFreuov3nqWbgN2gYgz7ZoUV3XF6Am7qc6HtWMrdWlKJmwG2sWoM9BaH8nXVeUz9t6NdyNFy7qUi7FubhcLbatUHYTuSQDfOrjnTy-vC4eGNmExEgFJ5Y5m4EFgFLwJK0uyda_XGdaJwNYtXig49Ksy4Kj5KzsUuGKg6iT_O0X-by1bIYW0zzo58o1oLUf1kF8yD7O9BV_VV6fU1U6giYvZ3t3tDWLFq-9C4QVGxfEAw-ZXQDqTMwk3GFVRP0GxH-iwHYmvZ9cH5khoYIWBX8z6zplppyoxCyNQNonQAF4UiGRXFS_9mFl9-ZhVym_oi5hAl6Tn9VD_TAHs_ofp_5xdlT-v6L9rU3qQnEUMkH_XrS34FRw_M956V-VuLJfWVb70qcClN1ZiLQYqbLgXq1DUwaDypK-pHM8XDomZX_EzOoQzk9HGjaTaNxXjMvd7gaB5ya7yjylBDJi8_-R5rQ%3D%3D)
Folks might've killed to have my job.
I was a sideline reporter for pro football and basketball. I covered some of the most exciting games in history. I watched sports for a living. And I loved every minute, every touchdown, and every Hail Mary.
I reached the pinnacle of my career... but there was one problem:
I had to watch what I said. I was a public-facing representative for a world-class sports network. I couldn't share everything I believed, and no one really knew I was a Conservative.

On Monday night, I got kicked out of the Charleston chapter of the DSA's "Childwatch Volunteer Training." The event was virtual and free to join. Since I recently attended my **[first DSA meeting last weekend](https://substack.com/redirect/53f4d370-76d1-41da-89c4-267963f57b89?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** and took DSA 101, I figured that the next step in my inclusion into the DSA would be as a volunteer.

Besides, I was curious to find out why the DSA felt the need to have specific programs targeting children. I was kicked out of the Zoom call as soon as they saw my USA t-shirt, which seems a little brash for a party that claims to be dedicated to "diversity, equity, and inclusion." Since I was removed from the call, I decided to dig in and find out what the DSA wants to do to children.
Last week, the Charleston chapter of the DSA **[announced](https://substack.com/redirect/069366ce-b0eb-40ed-ac8a-04d65231469b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** it would be holding a volunteer training for its childcare program, vowing to "Grow and support our next generation of comrades." The training session was intended to prepare volunteers to interact with children, describing activities such as "Roleplay through scenarios."

* * *
* * *
In **[March](https://substack.com/redirect/344de23c-8c61-4894-920d-36a14bfafd42?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** , the same chapter hosted a "Comrades With Kids" social event, which they hoped would be the "first of many" and a chance for families to build solidarity among families. "We'll order food to share, set up board games and card games, play some games out in the grass, and bring a few crafts to do with kids," Said the DSA. One of the stated goals of the event was to "Build a chapter that's welcoming of all ages."
The DSA National Political Education Committee began sponsoring "Child Watch" programs as far back as 2022. Their **[goal](https://substack.com/redirect/a54501df-1c7a-48c9-9af6-8ee545ff9e43?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** was to make DSA events "Accessible to children." According to DSA Childwatch volunteers, the nuclear family is a threat because it is too "isolating," mandating the need for collective care. Further, they have also stated that building childcare programs will allow DSA members to continue attending events, going to protests, and running for office.
* * *
* * *
### Support The Capitalist by getting the SubStack App
[Get the App](https://substack.com/redirect/adc6d5ea-28a2-470d-9a5a-23d666efcadd?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
* * *
* * *
In one of their **[previously recorded trainings](https://substack.com/redirect/0173105e-db02-4142-b334-9a9bfc7951b5?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** , they discussed how they wanted to change traditional childcare norms and to give adults "who haven't had the opportunity to interact with children a positive experience with them." Their stated goal was to build positive associations between young children and socialism. Several of the volunteers in charge of organizing the childcare services stated that they didn't have children but that they were "trying to build little socialists and organize them at a young age." Instructors asked volunteers to use "leftist coloring books and leftist children's books," and to prepare by reading "indigenous parenting books" that encouraged children to raise themselves, maintain "their own autonomy", and determine their own bedtime.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/b4b8f4ba-0fa0-43ad-ae5d-2c9cb0279bc3?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
The 2022 Childwatch training program instructed volunteers to replicate the structure of Sunday Schools "but without the religious programming... which is kinda whack." These indicate that they are reminiscent of the "Socialist Sunday Schools" created by radical cells in the early 20th century. They were designed to be alternatives to traditional Christian Sunday Schools, meeting at the same time as church services and sometimes aggregating as many as 150 students in urban centers. Teachers designed lesson plans that tried to undermine the singular power of a "bourgeois" God. A Socialist Sunday School teacher from Newark, Frederick Krafft, wrote that powerful figures "always become great either by deception, brutality, or some other evil propensity."
Children were taught about the value of globalism, the need for prison abolition, and were asked to compare the works of Karl Marx and Abraham Lincoln. The 2022 volunteers were instructed to do something similar, recommending that children be taught about progressive figures like Frida Kahlo. DSA Childwatch volunteers also extensively discussed how gender inequality played a role in traditional childcare, criticizing childcare for typically being a "role assigned to women." Their hope was to minimize the role of gender in childcare programs.
The DSA Childwatch programs are trying to indoctrinate children. At the end of the 2022 meeting, one leader excitedly exclaimed: "The babies want justice of the global liberation of the entire working class!"

They didn't have children but that they were "trying to build little socialists and organize them at a young age." | | | Aug 26| | | ∙| | Guest post ---|---|--- | | | | | | | | | | | | | | ---|---|--- The Capitalist exists because of you, and we want to hear from you! On Monday night, I got kicked out of the Charleston chapter of the DSA's "Childwatch Volunteer Training." The event was virtual and free to join. Since I recently attended my and took DSA 101, I figured that the next step in my inclusion into the DSA would be as a volunteer. | | | | ---|---|--- | Aug 19 | Besides, I was curious to find out why the DSA felt the need to have specific programs targeting children. I was kicked out of the Zoom call as soon as they saw my USA t-shirt, which seems a little brash for a party that claims to be dedicated to "diversity, equity, and inclusion." Since I was removed from the call, I decided to dig in and find out what the DSA wants to do to children. Last week, the Charleston chapter of the DSA it would be holding a volunteer training for its childcare program, vowing to "Grow and support our next generation of comrades." The training session was intended to prepare volunteers to interact with children, describing activities such as "Roleplay through scenarios." Its primary season and the DSA is on the rise inside the Democratic Party. But will the fervor that got Mamdani elected in New York translate into wins nationally? | | ---|---|--- Will there be a DSA "Revolution" or do they scare even Democrat voters? Get $25 in credit on Kalshi after you sign up using our code "brawl" or by In , the same chapter hosted a "Comrades With Kids" social event, which they hoped would be the "first of many" and a chance for families to build solidarity among families. "We'll order food to share, set up board games and card games, play some games out in the grass, and bring a few crafts to do with kids," Said the DSA. One of the stated goals of the event was to "Build a chapter that's welcoming of all ages." The DSA National Political Education Committee began sponsoring "Child Watch" programs as far back as 2022. Their was to make DSA events "Accessible to children." According to DSA Childwatch volunteers, the nuclear family is a threat because it is too "isolating," mandating the need for collective care. Further, they have also stated that building childcare programs will allow DSA members to continue attending events, going to protests, and running for office. Support The Capitalist by getting the SubStack App In one of their , they discussed how they wanted to change traditional childcare norms and to give adults "who haven't had the opportunity to interact with children a positive experience with them." Their stated goal was to build positive associations between young children and socialism. Several of the volunteers in charge of organizing the childcare services stated that they didn't have children but that they were "trying to build little socialists and organize them at a young age." Instructors asked volunteers to use "leftist coloring books and leftist children's books," and to prepare by reading "indigenous parenting books" that encouraged children to raise themselves, maintain "their own autonomy", and determine their own bedtime. | | ---|---|--- The 2022 Childwatch training program instructed volunteers to replicate the structure of Sunday Schools "but without the religious programming... which is kinda whack." These indicate that they are reminiscent of the "Socialist Sunday Schools" created by radical cells in the early 20th century. They were designed to be alternatives to traditional Christian Sunday Schools, meeting at the same time as church services and sometimes aggregating as many as 150 students in urban centers. Teachers designed lesson plans that tried to undermine the singular power of a "bourgeois" God. A Socialist Sunday School teacher from Newark, Frederick Krafft, wrote that powerful figures "always become great either by deception, brutality, or some other evil propensity." Children were taught about the value of globalism, the need for prison abolition, and were asked to compare the works of Karl Marx and Abraham Lincoln. The 2022 volunteers were instructed to do something similar, recommending that children be taught about progressive figures like Frida Kahlo. DSA Childwatch volunteers also extensively discussed how gender inequality played a role in traditional childcare, criticizing childcare for typically being a "role assigned to women." Their hope was to minimize the role of gender in childcare programs. The DSA Childwatch programs are trying to indoctrinate children. At the end of the 2022 meeting, one leader excitedly exclaimed: "The babies want justice of the global liberation of the entire working class!" Lead Story · Election IntegritySUPREME COURT CLEARS TRUMP'S MAIL-BALLOT ORDER — THEN A JUDGE SAYS THE POSTAL SERVICE JUMPED THE GUNWhat's Happening
* On Monday the Supreme Court lifted the injunction blocking President Trump's **“election integrity” executive order** on mail-in voting, ahead of the November midterms.
* Fox News reported the vote was **6-3** , with Justices Sotomayor, Kagan and Jackson dissenting. The Washington Examiner's account of the same emergency-docket ruling did not give a vote breakdown.
* The blocked order had been enjoined in **23 states** that sued — 23 Democrat-led states and the District of Columbia, per the Examiner — under a June order from U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani.
* The unsigned ruling turned on standing: the order “imposes no obligations on the States, so they 'suffer no concrete harm from' it.” The Court explicitly did _not_ rule on whether the order itself is lawful.
* A day later, Talwani found the Postal Service **violated her Aug. 11 preliminary injunction** by sending its final rule to the Federal Register on Friday with an immediate effective date: “Defendants cannot contend that they misunderstood the scope of the court's order.”

The Situation
* Talwani declined to impose further remedies sought by the League of Women Voters of Massachusetts, leaving the rule on track to publish Wednesday.
* Her injunction still bars the Postal Service from enforcing the new requirements for the **Nov. 3 election** or rejecting non-compliant ballot mail.
* The rule would have states hand USPS lists of voters who received mail ballots and require unique barcodes on outgoing and return ballot envelopes. The administration says USPS would _not_ determine whether any voter is eligible.
* The ruling also clears a path for USPS to check its ballot distribution against a citizenship list maintained by the Department of Homeland Security.
* An important caveat: Fox News noted it “has not reviewed any particular case of election fraud” tied to the Los Angeles mayoral primary the President has cited. Procedural vulnerabilities are not the same thing as proven fraud.

The PerspectiveConfirming that a ballot goes to a real, eligible voter is not voter suppression — it is the least a country can ask of its own mail system, and the Court was right that states cannot sue over a policy that does not yet bind them. But conservatives should want this done cleanly. The Postal Service getting slapped for blowing past a judge's order two months before an election is exactly the kind of self-inflicted wound that lets critics call the whole effort a power grab. Follow the process, win in court, and let the results speak.[Read the full story at Fox News](https://link.mail.beehiiv.com/ss/c/u001.SfPhhFqVdCCzAqIAosiI_NRx3TmKyUjNZ_2a-If6mreElYBBKMO3K8otUzLmfu0sTJTGgGT_eBnL1B6tMyKwvaYG6Qgw2JtqFbMiGF6fzrecyU57JlUmXBNNDysfE8qmn53WH_LPks2Khv1NiaIr7MaZ9g2ocGhJAxz7dXL5H4unnBMCn45m1P00N0tNe-mMKeCY8iuQKjsKh-kH_wTHjBgP7LKBZglLYL_bPl6Mtu6NgytOT-lBbG04kk6omCdi_wew-R72ULnIzVDw6thGr9wDmyB5hunXoDkSGZJWWggpxQj_bK5dZ3GacInzZ9lHTSEcdWJ6RL1Thg7w70semW-hjh32lAyTK0Y__iKEPIwMDMnx1NHvFxukOAcu_NZg/4ti/afkpKp8ATrSrJLCc6CUcTA/h5/h001.7xbxnSqWGDamLMs5fCauf7zEZYBHpKxlHmlYwRq8iQ4)

TradeCANADA TALKS COLLAPSE, 50% TARIFFS LAND — AND BORDER-STATE REPUBLICANS SQUIRMWhat's Happening
* Trade negotiations with Canada fell apart over the weekend. Two sets of tariffs have been threatened or imposed since Saturday, when the first round took effect.
* The second round is **50%** and takes effect **Jan. 1, 2027** — after the midterms. The covered goods are reported differently: Fox News lists automobiles, auto parts, trucks and steel; the Washington Examiner lists electronics, dairy products and vehicle parts.
* Trump on Monday: “Canada has been ripping off the United States of America for years.” On Tuesday he posted that the U.S. is giving “serious consideration” to renaming Lake Ontario **“Lake America.”**
* Vice President JD Vance, in Brewer, Maine, on Monday: “They treat Chinese goods more fairly than they do the goods that come from the people of Maine: It's insanity.”
* White House spokesman Kush Desai: “Canada tore up an incredibly generous and fair trade deal with the Trump administration.”

The Situation
* Sen. Susan Collins (R-ME) called the new tariffs a “mistake” on Saturday and urged both sides back to the negotiating table.
* Republicans hold a **three-seat Senate majority** , and more than a half-dozen of the closest 2026 races sit in states that border Canada — Michigan, Ohio, Maine and Alaska among them.
* Why the talks broke down is genuinely disputed. The White House blames last-minute Canadian demands; Ottawa levels the same charge at Washington.
* Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada walked because “we were not prepared to compromise on the protection of the French language and our culture.” U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer called that a “funny, fake story,” saying the American objection concerned requirements affecting U.S. streaming companies. Carney's account is a foreign government's characterization, not an established fact.
* Ontario Premier Doug Ford has urged retaliation aimed at “deep red states” so that America's economy “feels the pain.” Trump called Ford a “flunky.”

The PerspectiveCanada has spent decades protecting its own producers while lecturing Washington about free trade, and a president willing to say so out loud is overdue. The harder question is one conservatives should be honest about: tariffs are leverage, not a business model, and the delay to January 2027 tells you the White House knows the bill arrives after the ballots are counted. Republicans in Maine and Michigan have to answer for grocery and parts prices in the meantime. ImmigrationSTATE DEPARTMENT WEIGHS PULLING VISAS FROM UP TO 200,000 ASYLUM APPLICANTSWhat's Happening
* The administration is reportedly preparing to revoke business and tourist visas held by as many as **200,000 foreigners** who later applied for asylum in the United States.
* The effort would target **B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026**. If carried out, it would be the largest mass visa revocation in U.S. history.
* State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott: “We are coordinating with DHS to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently.”
* Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau posted Monday: “People in the US and all over the world are fed up with bogus asylum claims. Asylum isn't supposed to be a loophole to circumvent immigration law.”
* The State Department has revoked roughly **175,000 visas over the past 18 months** , according to The Associated Press.

The Situation
* Nothing has been announced. Reporting says a rollout is expected “in the coming weeks.”
* The 200,000 figure comes from the AP, citing internal documents and two U.S. officials. Pigott would not confirm a number, saying revocations would happen on a “rolling basis” and the total remained “dynamic.” Treat it as a projection.
* Revocation would not automatically trigger immediate deportations.
* People with pending asylum cases would generally be reclassified, but would lose their status as business or tourist travelers.
* Because the action is pre-decisional, both the scope and the legal mechanics could change before anything is signed.

The PerspectiveA visitor visa is a promise to visit. Filing for asylum the moment you land is not a technicality, it is a different application than the one the United States approved — and a system that never checks the difference invites exactly the abuse it got. Enforcing the terms of a visa is the most basic form of immigration enforcement there is. That said, 200,000 files is a staggering amount of case-by-case work, and some of those claims will be legitimate. Do it individually, document it, and let it survive the courts — because a sweep this size will be in front of a judge within the week.[Read the full story at Fox News](https://link.mail.beehiiv.com/ss/c/u001.SfPhhFqVdCCzAqIAosiI_NRx3TmKyUjNZ_2a-If6mrdMgnqzjaub68X5IYt-gAktNAytEKGrqjnT0ct1hsN-Fr0kBKeVRfHg6DDwX_wO50cWm7Jlw9MrgKhyBpMShaBq9lUJ4s1pg3SQ-6Y57UBwtUBeNPEcxclGYb-8iPEAKPWAR8yXBjAh77cozPc8AGF0zlv8tJyiN4-V9rO97ti8Wmc--KdV5zDYbuEejIG49Bm5puWmCyCArSd2rXMVpsS3rLNCJRJE-G_f7Z2KQAjDyc4ylVrmuSTYzi0IC_niHNSIjyuF1dXD-Stjw6IyhqlvJ18cjEBmrSl3qfN-SfxAKtWBo790x6JPxwzbhbQq1N-_v4VrMR8dmXjYyc6jfPhm/4ti/afkpKp8ATrSrJLCc6CUcTA/h7/h001.cq-s20rHXsWvGHEMowos5E2CItXqtSGTNZDVyb48SFc)

The Economy31 STATES ARE NOW OVER $4 A GALLON AS THE IRAN CAMPAIGN GRINDS ONWhat's Happening
* The national average for regular gasoline was **$4.097 a gallon** on Monday, according to AAA — up from $4.065 the week before.
* **31 states** now post a statewide average above $4 a gallon.
* The 2026 low was **$2.79 in January** ; the 2026 high was **$4.56, set in May**. The average has held between $4.05 and $4.11 for about a month.
* Most expensive: California **$5.623** , Hawaii $5.412, Washington $5.268. Least expensive: Indiana **$3.49** , Texas $3.62, South Carolina $3.64.
* Prices began climbing after **Operation Epic Fury** opened on Feb. 28, topping $4.50 by late winter.

The Situation
* Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced Monday an expansion of Iran sanctions plus secondary sanctions on countries whose banks and firms keep doing business with Tehran, calling it the “economic asphyxiation of this regime.”
* Trump said Tuesday that U.S. naval forces had cleared sea mines from the **Strait of Hormuz** , easing the flow of oil through the waterway.
* Secretary of State Marco Rubio has told allies the U.S. will hold off on striking Tehran “for the time being” and lean on the sanctions campaign instead. That account comes from U.S. officials who spoke to Axios and has not been confirmed on the record by the State Department.

* Strikes reportedly remain on the table if Iran moves first, with the broader plan holding until after the midterms.

The PerspectiveSqueezing the regime that has spent forty years funding attacks on Americans is the right call, and clearing mines out of Hormuz is the kind of quiet competence that never gets a headline. But nobody should pretend it is free. Four dollars a gallon in thirty-one states is a real cost carried by real families, and the honest conservative position is to say so out loud rather than wait for the other side to. | ⚡ The Bottom LineFour stories, one pattern: this administration is winning the arguments it picks and then daring the calendar to catch up with it. The mail-ballot order survived the Supreme Court but the Postal Service still has a judge on its neck. The tariffs land after Election Day. The visa revocations are still on a whiteboard. And gas is over four dollars in thirty-one states while the pressure on Iran does its slow work. None of that is failure — it is the cost of doing hard things in public, seventy days out from an election. Conservatives don't need to spin it. Win the cases, publish the numbers, and let voters weigh the bill against the results. That's just the truth.

**Part I: The CNN Confrontation --When a Host Becomes a Prosecutor**
In the summer of 2026, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. sat for an interview with CNN's Dana Bash that was supposed to examine America's lingering health crises. Instead, it became an object lesson in how mainstream media treated dissenting professionals during and after the pandemic. Rather than engaging substantively with Kennedy's policy positions, Bash's line of questioning repeatedly focused on challenging vaccine orthodoxy itself. Kennedy pushed back hard, telling Bash she was merely "repeating like a parrot" establishment talking points and challenging her to cite "one study that shows" vaccines significantly protected children--an answer that never came in the exchange. The interview quickly devolved into crosstalk, with Kennedy accusing CNN of having been "part of the problem" during the Biden-era COVID-19 response.

If conservatives turn out in November, we'll win every critical battleground and lay the groundwork for victory in 2028 and beyond.

That's why Turning Point Action is focusing all our efforts on three key states: Arizona, Nevada, and New Hampshire.

After 2024, Charlie looked at the numbers, looked at the maps, and told our team something simple. If we lock down Arizona, Nevada, and New Hampshire, the Left's entire strategy falls apart. Their map collapses. Their path back to power disappears.

Whoever wins in 2028 controls the 2030 Census. The Census drives redistricting. Redistricting sets the congressional map for the next ten years.

This midterm decides which way that goes.

| | | | | | | | | | | | | | |

Friends,Last night, approximately **120 Johnson County citizens** showed up for the Revenue Neutral Rate hearing. **Thirty-five spoke, and all but one asked the Commission not to pass the budget as is.** We heard heartbreaking stories, including a widow afraid rising property taxes may force her from her home, a veteran who has made our county her home, but is considering moving out of state and a brave county employee asking the Commission to **hold the budget flat.** And what did we hear in response?More half-truths. More shell games. More explanations for why spending cannot be reduced.But according to the County’s own handout, setting next year’s levy at the Revenue Neutral Rate would mean collecting **$19.8 million less in property taxes.** On a $1.9 billion budget, that is roughly **1%.** Even compared with actual expenditures, it is only about **1.4%.****Are we really supposed to believe they cannot find 1.4% in savings?** Not through vacant positions. Not through lower-priority projects. Not through greater efficiency. Not by simply prioritizing.**I don’t buy it.** Last night, citizens sent a clear message: **enough.** But, once again 6 of the 7 commissioners didn’t listen and voted to exceed RNR.We can have an extraordinary county and exercise fiscal discipline. Johnson County taxpayers deserve a Commission willing to do the hard work to make both happen. I am CONFIDENT of this.But...I need help.Every $25, $50, $100, or $250 contribution helps us reach another voter, put another sign in the ground, send another piece of mail, and make the case for a different direction in Johnson County.[**DONATE HERE**](https://us.list-manage.com/jKLbpy6KZBK?e=7320325a61&c2id=7adf4106091b2bdf32986c5b36d3a494) And money alone will not win this election.We are building an army of supporters who believe Johnson County deserves transparent leadership, fiscal sanity, accountability, and a government that remembers whose money it is spending.Knock doors. Make calls. Host a gathering. Put up a sign. Talk to your neighbors.[**JOIN THE TEAM**](https://us.list-manage.com/yO0iNKKFCse?e=7320325a61&c2id=7adf4106091b2bdf32986c5b36d3a494) I promise to fight to bring about positive change and fiscal sanity. **Are you ready to join me?** Respectfully,
Karen Crnkovich
Candidate for Johnson County Commission Chair

body:
And now, I’m carrying his legacy with me each and every single day.
| | | | | [](https://eub669hbb.cc.rs6.net/tn.jsp?f=0019uc6ih66es8igt-jfju312gW8Hg2E0Qv-MLhh0elW-V25oNeKSMcYPkqY8OMk0NdTKNhwkCAL6LBxYyg4zZ8OlLOpMPgg91Gb3dRugVwVBVdJO4rAMGdXhwoj7gOC0Xo8L2FbdhG7Zz0OK3zJg4K-NTbAGYNHaq2Kzi5zFNzkAca8O-PvHwCRanIC7LcLglN4K9AbchMfko8eqsgvLQJCNB-Wiq46yunffUI8hlRSOk=&c=myE_Q1RFdp2Yg4aut0wfxY_gAEOElcgEzi22YeIxbKvjodxDhWIoaw==&ch=MFYHKrsYnNvUfLsGsmJbrtZNYSHpneULhBHZTfcjOelEJNpMOM7EmQ==)
---
| Peter,
My grandfather was a sharecropper.
He worked the land from sunup to sundown that he would never own. He picked cotton by hand in the brutal Louisiana heat, breaking his body for a system designed to keep him exactly where he was -- poor, powerless, and dependent on the landowners who controlled everything.
That was life in the Louisiana Delta. My father grew up in that world. In those days in rural Louisiana, many boys left school early because their families needed them in the fields.
Work came first.
But my Dad had a dream that his son wouldn't have to live that way. That somehow, some way, our family would own land instead of working someone else's. That we'd build something that couldn't be taken away.
And he did it. Through decades of backbreaking work, he made that dream real.
We started with 220 acres my father had leased and built it into something real, something ours.
Today, we farm over 3,200 acres. 700 of those acres belong to my family outright.
Some of the same Louisiana delta soil my grandfather worked as a sharecropper -- my family owns it now.
Do you understand how profound that is? How impossible that would have seemed to my grandfather?
And now I'm running to become Louisiana's first Black senator since Reconstruction.
Sometimes I think about what my grandfather would say if he could see this moment. A man living in a system designed to keep him down, whose grandson might represent this entire state in the United States Senate.
It takes my breath away.
This isn't just about me. It's about every Black family in America that was told they'd never amount to anything. Every sharecropper's descendant who was supposed to stay in their place. Every person who was counted out before they even got started.
If I win this seat, it won't erase the centuries of injustice that came before. It won't undo what was done to my grandfather or the millions like him.
But it will prove something powerful: that in Louisiana -- in the Deep South -- we can move forward. That the grandson of a sharecropper can stand as an equal in the halls of power. That our democracy, for all its flaws, can still bend toward justice.
My grandfather never got to see this. My father -- God rest his soul -- never got to see this either.
But my grandkids will. And maybe, just maybe, they'll grow up in a Louisiana where anything truly is possible, regardless of the color of your skin or which side of the tracks you were born on.
That's what this campaign means to me. It's personal in a way I can barely put into words.
And I need your help to make it real.

| Friend,

I do not usually write long emails, but I want to lay out the whole picture, because you deserve to see how far this has gone.

The Democrat Party you grew up with is gone. What replaced it is a socialist movement that is winning, and winning big. They elected a Ugandan-born, radical socialist as mayor of New York City. In Michigan, a Bernie Sanders Islamist radical just ripped a United States Senate nomination away from the party establishment. From New York to Colorado to Michigan, they are throwing out their own incumbent Democrats for the crime of not being far enough to the left. body:
| |
---
Peter -- I want to tell you what it feels like to find out you can win. Recently, we released half our poll -- the dead heat. Here's the half we didn't release. Blueprint told voters who I am. Twenty years in the Navy. Fourteen on submarines. Command Master Chief. Then home to South Carolina to run a small business. They told them what I'm fighting for, and they told them Russell Fry's record. Then they asked again, who would you support? **John Vincent 48%. Russell Fry 37%.** I read that number about six times. For years, people in this district have been told to sit down. That the seat is safe, the math doesn't work, don't waste your time. Every one of us has heard it. Some of us started to believe it. Peter,
**People are waking up — and it should have Republicans and the establishment everywhere terrified.**
Across the country, voters are rejecting the captured politicians who have been collecting corporate checks and special interest money for decades while the very corporations funding them make working people’s lives harder to survive.
Voters see the writing on the wall, and they’re energized to go to the polls and choose something better.
**That’s why we keep winning in races we’re being outspent in — _because the messages our candidates are carrying matter more than a corporate check.**_
Thanks to your support, we’ve been able to move the needle every single day and prove that working class politics is the way to win.
Just look at **Patrick Roath** ’s race. Since last month, he’s surged _15%_ in the polls against 25-year incumbent Stephen Lynch — a conservative, do-nothing Democrat who has repeatedly failed to meet this moment with the urgency it demands. Patrick’s election is right around the corner on **September 1** , and he’s within single digits of his opponent. We have _5 days_ to get him across the finish line.
Also on September 1, **Daniel Lander** is taking on a 14-year incumbent in Massachusetts who has spent years blocking the affordability agenda working families in his district desperately need.
These are exactly the kind of candidates Leaders We Deserve was built to back.
Peter, with your support, we can continue the momentum we’ve built and keep securing wins to flip seats red-to-blue and primary asleep-at-the-wheel Democrats in safe blue seats.
