Last year, my husband survived 124 days inside the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma. He's a 100% disabled American military veteran in a wheelchair. Nearly 30 years in this country, served honorably, never broken a law -- not even a parking ticket. He never should have been there.
A federal judge ordered his release, calling his detention "flat out wrong." We won.
But I know that building now. The visiting cubicles where you sit across from someone you love, separated by glass, forbidden to touch. The guards who chatted about weekend barbecues while deciding whether I could see my husband. And what happened inside: medical neglect, food so bad one breakfast was half a cup of cornflakes and a scoop of leftover mashed potatoes, a fellow detainee who collapsed while guards shouted my husband -- a trained paramedic -- away from CPR. By the time help arrived, the brain damage was permanent.
Washington State fought for years to inspect this facility. GEO fought it to the Ninth Circuit and lost. A federal judge ordered the doors opened in July 2026.
Then within weeks, ICE started looking to buy a facility matching NWIPC exactly. GEO told investors it's negotiating sales and publicly described federal ownership as a way around state oversight.
They lost the argument that GEO should be treated like the federal government -- so now the federal government may buy the building. That's the move.
GEO gets paid for the property. GEO keeps getting paid to run the prison. The people behind the glass stay under the same private management. And oversight? The part inspectors can see simply gets smaller and smaller until it exists mostly on paper.
I'll be watching the procurement records, GEO's disclosures, Pierce County filings, and whatever agreement accompanies this sale. My family already learned what happens when a human being disappears behind those walls and accountability cannot reach him.
My job is to end this so no family has to go through it again.
Care. Courage. The Constitution.

Now let me tell you why this mission means so much to me. My name is Eduardo Verastegui. Several years ago, I learned firsthand about the horrific reality of child trafficking. What I heard broke my heart. Children were being bought and sold.
Families were being torn apart.
Lives were being destroyed. **I couldn't forget it.** **I couldn't stay silent.** I kept asking myself one question: **"What if it were my child?"** That question changed my life. What started as a film project became a mission and a calling. That calling eventually led me to help produce the film _Sound of Freedom_. **Not for fame.**
**Not for awards.**
**But because I believed people needed to see the truth.** For years, many people said the film would never succeed. Doors closed.
Studios walked away.
People told us to give up. **But when innocent children are suffering, silence is not an option.** And while the film helped awaken millions of people to this crisis, awareness alone is not enough. That is why we created the **Sound of Freedom Foundation**. Our mission is simple: **To stop the sale of God's children.**

Meet Joe Males:

**Joe Males is a Marine Veteran, small business-owner, city council member, and most importantly, a father. Throughout his life, he has put service to his community at the forefront of his life’s mission.

Shortly after turning 18, Joe enlisted in the Marine Corps. He attended boot camp in Camp Pendleton and later served overseas in the Philippines and Guam. He took on leadership roles in his local Elks Lodge and American Legion post, working to ensure veterans in the community had the resources and support they deserved.

Following his time in the Marine Corps, Joe carried his strong work ethic and discipline into the field of computer networking services. He started in an entry-level position, worked his way through multiple leadership roles, and in 1996, he built his own business from the ground up. Joe knows firsthand the hard work and sacrifice of this journey, and he’s determined to make it easier for hardworking Americans to do the same.

Joe’s entry into politics was deeply personal. After his son, a Marine who followed in his footsteps, was tragically murdered back home, Joe vowed that no parent should have to endure such a loss. Determined to take a stand for public safety and the rule of law, he ran for Hemet City Council to help ensure no other family would experience the same tragedy.

During his tenure on the City Council, Joe has led numerous initiatives to improve infrastructure, drive business growth, and keep neighborhoods safe and clean. He takes pride in his ability to collaborate with fellow council members and get results, even when facing different perspectives. Joe is committed to bringing this same results-driven approach to Washington D.C., to ensure the voices of the American people are heard and their needs are met.

The president’s latest tantrum
#

**Trump really can’t help himself.**
Within hours of my Senate race being called, the president had an unhinged tantrum on Truth Social — saying I “should be prosecuted” for standing up to his corruption.
[](https://secure.actblue.com/donate/av-em-troyjackson?refcode=em260825&refcode2=1083_3892029_NdldDD&akid=1083%2E3892029%2ENdldDD)
Here’s the difference between Donald Trump and me: I can accept the results of a free and fair election. I don’t need to stage an insurrection to protect my ego.
But if Donald Trump thought this was going to get me to shut up and stay on the sidelines of this essential fight, then I have two words for him:
Hell no.
**Today, my campaign is contributing $7,500 to Democrat Troy Jackson’s campaign. The easiest path for a Democratic Senate majority runs through Maine, and Troy’s opponent is Republican Susan Collins.**
If you are pissed off about the direction of our country, a lot of it can be traced back to Susan Collins. She voted with Trump 95% of the time last year, even though the people of Maine rejected him in 2016, 2020, and 2024.
Troy can win this thing. He’s a fifth-generation logger, lifelong fighter for workers’ rights, and has a proven record of winning in places that voted for Donald Trump. But he’s not taking a penny from corporate PACs — so he needs all of our help to win this thing.

| | _With just thirteen days until the primary, I am using each day to discuss an issue I have highlighted on the campaign trail. For Day 13, I am highlighting the need to raise the minimum wage to make life more affordable for families._
* * *
Dear David, Here’s a not-so-fun fact about New Hampshire: Our minimum wage is still tied to the federal minimum wage. **The federal minimum wage hasn’t budged in years _(it’s only $7.25 an hour!)_ , which means New Hampshire’s minimum wage is still... $7.25 an hour.** **[It costs $8.50 to do a load of laundry in the big machine on Route 1 in Hampton, so it’s safe to say that we need to raise the minimum wage if we want people to be able to afford to live here. If you’re ready to make sure that people are making a livable wage, please pitch in today:](https://go.sparkpostmail1.com/f/a/UhGqq7n4hZubde1WCKarZA~~/AAUS1hA~/PpBGBUzLk3pPKH16FOnPo3HsdFweDS634QqYh7AERajlcYPCfOtS8dzug9YdYlABpt9HfYeOys3fn6fZB4Sjh27koQanZR0tcN9Yhfn6TT0trsg-TBtbILmByKVfN4Hce0wZjfp1JAWYVNT-b7eZkGZ0cnKhFgxBJEHybJU5fy1HmfPbCeTD4cXny_b21XtBvRi4w-N4OSFmnjqKHM_ZvujyWA41NbDZfQtTh_MnoP_JOPnSB20yQxcIZvJ5e-IwaRFM4ylasUE1HdOKZywwoA~~)** | | [DONATE](https://go.sparkpostmail1.com/f/a/UhGqq7n4hZubde1WCKarZA~~/AAUS1hA~/PpBGBUzLk3pPKH16FOnPo3HsdFweDS634QqYh7AERajlcYPCfOtS8dzug9YdYlABpt9HfYeOys3fn6fZB4Sjh27koQanZR0tcN9Yhfn6TT0trsg-TBtbILmByKVfN4Hce0wZjfp1JAWYVNT-b7eZkGZ0cnKhFgxBJEHybJU5fy1HmfPbCeTD4cXny_b21XtBvRi4w-N4OSFmnjqKHM_ZvujyWA41NbDZfQtTh_MnoP_JOPnSB20yQxcIZvJ5e-IwaRFM4ylasUE1HdOKZywwoA~~)
---
People should make enough money so they have the time to sit around the table with the people they love, give back to their communities, run for office, and participate in local government.
But that’s not possible when only making $7.25 an hour. **If we want people to make more money, we need to stand with workers organizing for fair pay, fair schedules, and the right to bargain.**
As a union organizer, I fought to form UAW Local 5118, a union of graduate student workers demanding fair pay, paid leave, transparent scheduling, and anti-retaliation policies. We went on strike _twice_ before securing our first contract.
[](https://go.sparkpostmail1.com/f/a/UhGqq7n4hZubde1WCKarZA~~/AAUS1hA~/PpBGBUzLk3pPKH16FOnPo3HsdFweDS634QqYh7AERajlcYPCfOtS8dzug9YdYlABpt9HfYeOys3fn6fZB4Sjh27koQanZR0tcN9Yhfn6TT0trsg-TBtbILmByKVfN4Hce0wZjfp1JAWYVNT-b7eZkGZ0cnKhFgxBJEHybJU5fy1HmfPbCeTD4cXny_b21XtBvRi4w-N4OSFmnjqKHM_ZvujyWA41NbDZfQtTh_MnoP_JOPnSB20yQxcIZvJ5e-IwaRFM4ylasUE1HdOKZywwoA~~)
I’ve also joined the picket line with members of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers (IBEW) Local 1837 to support them in their fight for a fair contract, and stood in solidarity with Starbucks workers fighting for the benefits they deserve.
Walking the picket line in the dead of winter and standing shoulder to shoulder with workers has taught me a lesson that I’ll bring to the halls of Congress: **Every worker deserves a union.**
**[That’s why I’ll proudly sign on to the PRO Act and fight to restore collective bargaining rights to 1.5 million federal workers hurt by Trump and Elon Musk’s DOGE disaster. If you believe, as I do, that our workers deserve benefits that reflect that hard work, pitch in to join me in the fight to secure workers’ rights and raise the minimum wage.](https://go.sparkpostmail1.com/f/a/UhGqq7n4hZubde1WCKarZA~~/AAUS1hA~/PpBGBUzLk3pPKH16FOnPo3HsdFweDS634QqYh7AERajlcYPCfOtS8dzug9YdYlABpt9HfYeOys3fn6fZB4Sjh27koQanZR0tcN9Yhfn6TT0trsg-TBtbILmByKVfN4Hce0wZjfp1JAWYVNT-b7eZkGZ0cnKhFgxBJEHybJU5fy1HmfPbCeTD4cXny_b21XtBvRi4w-N4OSFmnjqKHM_ZvujyWA41NbDZfQtTh_MnoP_JOPnSB20yQxcIZvJ5e-IwaRFM4ylasUE1HdOKZywwoA~~)**

Thank you, Fellow Patriot.

It's been a long six weeks, but because you were by my side, _we won._

Your generosity helped us through the Special Election Primary and through a head-to-head runoff.

**But that was just the first step to securing this seat.**

I am the first woman United States senator in South Carolina history. My Democratic opponent, Dr. Annie Andrews, cannot be the second.

Here's where the race stands. Two statewide elections in less than 6 weeks were expensive. We knew it would be a tough battle - it was.

We did not want to leave anything to chance, so we had to ensure every dollar we raised was well spent on television ads, voter contacts, and signs across South Carolina.

**[Our campaign coffers are empty after a well-fought battle.](http://links.ourdefenseofamerica.com/u/click?_t=aa3ef0db03454a26b650c9ca7e919386&_m=eb20a14226ed4cbba0c0ad30c2af4029&_e=-ij1HtyxFUH8fLsAoyPAdiS5hM-RD0165uUeuBhUK4U5cUUZwh4EMXTW-HEoQrtDdCCF2vsQVm5C3cG91XAz24vQD3Ztkw78PfqC-yKtIa6nFGBHORJhtHBLg5NglfN-uMLMjM5v4kHbhvH1jM0yuOqqkjplPh8gCl0ydxDglgrFMMDF_UzF_cTrCxwX3IojgIwG5gLEutPAKUTIZkSI2H-H8zkbv2Ne1-R-3AETWyr2YRHmHmjnGoDuNaIGb6DSZmcPIhBndKfg9DSNDSJmaB6plvokqGLucSR7JjrHVkYmjeS_Gk5Ei11zDbkpRoxK4XsaBX0B2Cp8XVGLQGUrbmZ5JwpQR97Vpe4mGUc-wPfobx0Qo47cfEWJniLzjhkLOb4niTvTouEpfIJcSoM79JeBpSGoyZC4nKF7_GRV6osq-u3_1QWRP_lqbJb7R7qiIc0L4F3u3X4v_9c4BheXba_NE14-7_MR_fUkb7PBgOdx907ncCAhL3ANpsU89DnGLN4f9lpaiOhbCkYakXZU1z69F222S6j8f_33RmR4s3kC_gvyVsSOP-EFryxQZorCqH1-llhHDfgDeNCxYfKxd8V_wqjHxKZWIFHrfR4sS4IvSdgfb5oXmbxxHMmdDMPN_0hVeKblOJZXuw-ZckXqrl8-PMwEhdY5oMhZBtgMdVgp3UTueNJ95y0guB9X8SEymKB_ehPGSYvi3tr-D5g1C5vK6x57CfinRVazlMOK1Lfbc9ByylhA8yDwn1MDowRWt14O2opXgJ3zB7NUIVQChg%3D%3D)**

We are starting at square one, going into the general election, and let me tell you about our Democrat opponent. She's raising millions from liberal donors who want nothing more than to flip this seat and stop President Trump's agenda in Washington.

_**I need your help again, Fellow Patriot.**_

Friend, As our families struggle to afford the daily basics of food, housing, and healthcare, we cannot afford another economic collapse or another taxpayer-funded bank bailout. **But until Congress acts, Big Bank executives will continue to be incentivized to take major financial risks that threaten everyone’s economic security.** That’s why I’ve introduced the **_Bank Failure Accountability Act_** to stop bank executives from getting huge payouts while breaking the law or leading their company to collapse. The bill requires large financial institutions to place a portion of senior employee compensation into a deferred fund, and that money would only be released if the firm doesn’t fail or commit misconduct over a certain period of time―between two and eight years, depending on the size of the institution. [**Protect the American people from the greed and recklessness of Big Bank executives who put risky short-term gains over everyone’s economic security. The 2008 financial crisis led to passage of _the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act_ , which among other things tasked federal regulators with banning executive compensation packages that encourage inappropriate risk-taking. But to this day, that provision in _Dodd-Frank_ is yet to be implemented.
More recently, the 2023 bank failures, beginning with the failure of Silicon Valley Bank, highlighted how misaligned executive incentives encourage risk taking that can give executives a huge short-term payout while harming the broader economy.
Time and time again, we have seen executives and senior employees at large financial institutions pursue short-term profits at any cost because their compensation packages encourage excessive risk-taking. **Executives pocket millions of dollars while workers and communities pay the price.**
[**Let’s hold Big Banks and their wealthy executives accountable. clean_body: The American people are tired of bank bailouts. | | | Friend, As our families struggle to afford the daily basics of food, housing, and healthcare, we cannot afford another economic collapse or another taxpayer-funded bank bailout. But until Congress acts, Big Bank executives will continue to be incentivized to take major financial risks that threaten everyone’s economic security. That’s why I’ve introduced the Bank Failure Accountability Act to stop bank executives from getting huge payouts while breaking the law or leading their company to collapse. The bill requires large financial institutions to place a portion of senior employee compensation into a deferred fund, and that money would only be released if the firm doesn’t fail or commit misconduct over a certain period of time―between two and eight years, depending on the size of the institution. | The 2008 financial crisis led to passage of the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act , which among other things tasked federal regulators with banning executive compensation packages that encourage inappropriate risk-taking. But to this day, that provision in Dodd-Frank is yet to be implemented. More recently, the 2023 bank failures, beginning with the failure of Silicon Valley Bank, highlighted how misaligned executive incentives encourage risk taking that can give executives a huge short-term payout while harming the broader economy. Time and time again, we have seen executives and senior employees at large financial institutions pursue short-term profits at any cost because their compensation packages encourage excessive risk-taking. Executives pocket millions of dollars while workers and communities pay the price. Thank you for taking action today to create a structure of accountability that disincentivizes bank executives’ worst behavior. Always serving you, Rashida Rashida Tlaib for Congress PO Box 32777 Detroit, MI 48232 | Paid for by Rashida Tlaib for Congress | | Sent via . * * *
Mamdani's socialist grocery stores are already backfiring big time and they're not even opened yet.
Imagine you're a young Cuban family who immigrated legally, or a couple from the midwest moving to the big city, or maybe a lifelong New Yorker born and raised. You start a small bodega under your apartment to earn a modest living. It's all you can afford, and even then, you're probably in debt up to your eyeballs. You begin to build a loyal customer base, and your profit margin is healthy but not large by any means.
Then you see a new sign go up across the street:
_" City-Run Grocery Store, Everything Is 30% Off!"_
Your livelihood is over.
This new store sells everything at a 30% discount. It isn't that your customers don't appreciate you; they just can't afford to pass up the price cuts.
You go bankrupt. Your family goes hungry.
...
The plan for Mayor Mamdani's government-run stores includes a 30% discount on prices and is estimated to save New Yorkers around $90 a month. Not nothing, but not worth it if it means destroying the local small business community.
And New Yorkers have made up their minds: They won't let a socialist take their businesses. That's why they are joining **[The Multicultural Business Coalition to sue Mamdani.](https://substack.com/redirect/8250f519-c4a4-44f3-a8b1-45a2580f74e6?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**
Mark Jaffe, the general counsel for the nonprofit, spelled out perfectly why Zohran will lose:
"You cannot expect hard-working small business owners to compete with a supermarket that isn't going to pay rent, won't have to pay an electric bill and won't have to buy their products at full price. They cannot possibly compete because no one will be subsidizing them."

* * *
When asked about the destructive policy, Mamdani admitted that not only was it economically illiterate, but it was pointless as well.
"We're talking about delivering five city-run grocery stores in a city of eight and a half million people that has more than 1,000 grocery stores," Mamdani said in a press conference.
He quite literally admitted that these grocery stores could have very little positive impact on the city, while still undercutting the local grocery stores around them.
No upside, a ton of downside.
Zohran already has a history of intentionally missing the forest for the trees. He's expanding rent control in New York City by 1 million units, making nearly half the city rent-controlled. While socialists believe rent control helps drive prices down, once again, it undercuts local businesses and stifles supply.
When landlords can't charge market rates for rent, they stop upgrading and fixing their properties, developers cease building, and prices end up rising everywhere else in the city. Zohran is undercutting local grocery stores in the same way.
New York's bodegas and local grocers are the heartbeat of this city, built by families who risked everything for a shot at the American dream. Mamdani's government-run grocery stores might promise a temporary discount, but the hidden cost is the total destruction of their neighborhoods' economic foundation.
The silver lining: Maybe this is the wake up call New Yorkers need to realize socialism is the poison, not the fix.

Fellow Patriot -

I never expected to be running for office. I have never had any desire to be a politician. I am doing this because I am answering President Donald Trump's call to serve and want to stand up for South Carolina and fight for his agenda.

_**Like Lindsey, I am a hard worker with a servant's heart.**_ We grew up in the back of a bar and liquor store, in one room. Our parents worked hard every day to make ends meet - there was no time for sickness and few vacations, because if the doors weren't open, no money was coming in.

What I've spent my life doing is serving South Carolina - including running a state agency with 130 employees and a $90 million budget. We turned it from a struggling organization into a national model helping people find work and live independently. Friend,

We need to be clear about what Women’s Equality Day means in 2026.

We are living through an era in which women are being delegitimized, silenced, and disenfranchised. From extreme judges gutting reproductive freedoms to far-right politicians trying to roll back equal pay protections and ignore a rising maternal health crisis, the message from the right is simple: know your place.

My answer? Not on my watch.

Join me in my fight against these unrelenting attacks on women's rights, bodily autonomy, and economic equality; chip in $15 or $25 today → [https://secure.actblue.com/donate/SEMD-03-Email-Aug2026-FR-WomenEquality?&refcode=E31373-20280826-WomenEquality-SL-Holiday&amount=15]

Growing up watching my mother work as a civil servant, I saw firsthand that women carry our communities on their backs. When I became the youngest woman ever elected to the Maryland Senate, I learned quickly that when you don’t have a seat at the table, you pull up a chair and make your voice heard louder.

The women who won the right to vote 106 years ago didn't ask for permission – and neither will we.

The ballot box is our ultimate weapon. We use it to demand equal pay for equal work, to pass guaranteed paid family leave, to save mothers' lives, and to protect our fundamental right to make our own health care decisions.

We owe it to the women who came before us, and the girls watching us now, to fight like hell against every single attempt to take our country backward.

Stand with me on Women’s Equality Day. Please chip in $25 right now to help us build a world where women don't just survive; we lead → [https://secure.actblue.com/donate/SEMD-03-Email-Aug2026-FR-WomenEquality?&refcode=E31373-20280826-WomenEquality-SL-Holiday&amount=25]

With strength and pride,

Sarah Elfreth

Congresswoman Sarah Elfreth broke barriers in 2024, becoming the youngest woman ever elected to Congress from Maryland. She went to Congress with one thing in mind: delivering for Maryland families on the issues that matter most. Whether it's standing up for federal workers, supporting veterans, protecting the Chesapeake Bay, or tackling the affordability crisis head-on, Sarah is on the front lines, fighting for what is right. And Sarah has delivered on her promises. She has spent her first year in the House advocating for the Third District, successfully passing five bills into law, solving over 1,000 constituent cases, and bringing tens of millions in funding back to her community. She learned her work ethic and tenacity from growing up in a union household and honed her skills of problem-solving and collaborating over six years in the Maryland State Senate. Team,The Supreme Court dropped another "shadow docket" ruling last night, this one **making it easier for Trump to implement his anti-mail-in voting Executive Order**.First: The "_shadow docket_." It's the Supreme Court's way to review cases quickly without formal hearings. It's a construct of the last few decades, not widely used previous to that, but tons of unsigned, pro-Trump rulings have been issued from the Supreme Court this way the last few years. This ruling, _offered on procedural grounds and not the merits of the law_ , was a short-term win for the Trump administration as they try to **use the Department of Homeland Security and the Postal Service to create a national voter registration list and usurp the constitutional authority of the states to run our elections**. Even if this is short-lived, **this is not good news.** Opponents of voting rights will take every inch they can in their battle to suppress votes and invalidate your ballot. name: OnePA Team
subject: Tell your Secretary of State not to give Trump our voter information
body:
State officials do not have to surrender voter information because Trump threatens our mail | |
---
Peter, **** The Trump administration is trying to strong-arm states into handing over sensitive information about people voting by mail. Under a proposed Postal Service rule, states would have to submit voters’ names, addresses, and identifying ballot barcode information to a new federal system before their ballot mail would be accepted. **Then Postmaster General David Steiner made the threat explicit.** When Senators asked whether the USPS would deliver election mail if states refused to turn over the information, Steiner said it would not. **In other words, give the Trump administration the voter information it wants, or risk having ballots rejected by the Postal Service.** **But our Secretaries of State need to understand something clearly: their hands are not tied.** While a Supreme Court decision lifted one injunction and led to the lifting of the nationwide injunction blocking the USPS from moving forward with Steiner’s plan, the Court did not decide whether Trump’s order or Steiner’s scheme is constitutional. Even if a new nationwide injunction is put in place after new court filings, the uncertainty while the legal cases are moving forward just strengthens the need for secretaries of state to act. **These threats to our voting rights only work if state officials let themselves be intimidated by it. Secretaries of State have the power and the responsibility to refuse Trump’s demand, protect our voter information, and make clear that every lawful ballot must be delivered. subject: We're working to bring your voice to the table.

body:

---
| | | [SDPB Article ](https://us.list-manage.com/UKqaZTrT8K0?e=cee7b49c04&c2id=3adc23449cf80dcda430cceaf3c4b05d)
---
| |
---
| | | |
---
| |
---
Meet my Lieutenant Governor, Steve McCleery

Good leadership means including perspectives that will broaden our understanding, challenge us, and open the door to collaboration that creates creative solutions that work for everyone. With his background in agriculture and legislation, Steve McCleery brings expertise and a valuable perspective that will allow us to holistically represent South Dakotans.

Steve has spent 20 years working as a dairy farmer, managing impressive cow/calf operations, along with row crop operations. He knows what Pierre owes to the people who feed this state and this nation, and he also knows the importance of property rights in the face of government overreach.

Steve has also had his share of talking policy in the state legislature, having served six years as a representative, working across the aisle to bridge division and get work done for South Dakotans.

The government should represent everybody; that’s a value that Steve and I stand for, and one we will continue to fight for on the campaign trail.

| | |
---
| |
---
Lawrence, Brown, and Charles Mix County Visits

Friendly crowds in counties across the state shared their insight, experiences, and concerns. I’m grateful to these hard working South Dakotans for taking time out of their day to speak with me. Whether we are East or West River, South Dakotans are worried about similar things. Common among them are properly funded schools, support for teachers, and access to childcare.

My experience as a substitute teacher has made it clear to me that we need leaders who speak about and treat our teachers with the respect and esteem they deserve. Likewise, our actions need to follow our words. For too long this state has neglected the financial needs of our educators and schools. As a result, many teachers have left the state and the profession entirely.

Our teachers and schools are core to the foundation of our community. When leaders treat teachers with respect and support, learning and behavioral outcomes are improved. Our children are better equipped for their future, and that’s how we achieve a brighter South Dakota.

| | | |
---
| |
---
Insights from the Great Plains Tribal Chairmen’s Association

I’m grateful to have been given the opportunity to hear from the Great Plains Tribal Chairmen’s Association about what they want from the gubernatorial office to address the pressing issues facing South Dakota’s tribes. Lack of funds and support, rising crime, an under-resourced police force, and cases involving MMIPs reamin unaddressed. The tribes have told us they are in crisis, and I have heard it loud and clear.

Active cooperation, resources, and mutual respect are what’s needed to improve the lives in our tribal communities. I believe that respect involves recognizing the sovereignty of native communities and working collaboratively to deliver the resources they need.

Good leadership treats everyone with respect and dignity. Creating solutions doesn’t stop at listening – it starts with including these voices at the table and following through with the commitments you made to those whom you chose to represent. The state must reflect its commitment to cooperation and building trust through action, not just words. As governor, this will be my framework for working with native communities.

| | |
---
| |
---
Citizens for Liberty Event

Thank you to the folks at Citizens for Liberty for organizing this great event. Opportunities to listen to South Dakotans from all communities and perspectives are vital to my campaign, and the engagement at this gathering was insightful.

I heard a lot of concern about waste and a lack of transparency within our state government. My experience as a small business owner taught me how to squeeze pennies into dimes. My time in the legislature taught me how to be a public servant that serves the people instead of chasing political distractions. I know how to create operations that are efficient, purposeful, and transparent. As governor, I will continue these processes to deliver solutions that work.

Restoring trust is a major facet of my campaign. Government works best when it welcomes scrutiny instead of avoiding it. That's the standard I will hold my office and the legislature to.

I look forward to visiting again, and to keep this important dialogue happening.

| | | |
---
| |
---
| |
---
Economic Development Should Start at Home

South Dakota needs an economic development strategy that invests in South Dakotans; not one that gives tens of millions of dollars to large, out-of-state companies while producing little economic benefit for our communities.

We recently provided $69 million to an out-of-state company that resulted in a couple hundred jobs paying about $18 an hour. That is a massive public investment for jobs paying wages that are comparable to what an individual can earn working in fast food in Sioux Falls. Supporters of these deals often point to the property tax revenue they generate. But we should ask a basic question: What is the economic benefit we are actually receiving for that investment? We could invest in affordable housing, create jobs through construction, and generate the same or greater property tax revenue while addressing a critical need in our communities.

Meanwhile, there are South Dakotans ready to build businesses right here at home.

While visiting Dakota Hemp in Wakonda, I met a farmer who is growing industrial hemp and wants to build a $3 million dollar factory to manufacture hempcrete. Hempcrete can be used in home construction and could become an important part of our affordable housing solutions. I asked him where he planned to build his plant. His answer was Iowa. When I asked why, he told me there were no economic incentives available to help him build it in South Dakota.

Think about that. For the same $69 million we invested in one out-of-state company, we could have supported 23 projects like his across South Dakota. His plant would employ 10 to 12 people earning $22 to $25 an hour, while creating a new market for a South Dakota agricultural product. And this kind of small-business development can happen in communities across our state.

As governor, I want to change our approach to economic development. We need to make it easier for South Dakota entrepreneurs, farmers and small businesses to start, expand and create good-paying jobs right here in our communities.

When we invest locally, more of that money stays locally. It supports local businesses, local workers, local farmers and local communities.

Economic development shouldn't just be about landing the biggest company. It should be about creating the greatest benefit for the people of South Dakota.

| | | |
---
| |
---
| |
---
Here’s where you can find me next.

| |
---
August 30th Latino Community Meet and Greet at the Augustana Lutheran Church, Sioux Falls

August 30th Brookings County Democrats Potluck Picnic, Brookings Activity Center

September 1st Super Tuesday with the Pennington County Dems at The Hive, Rapid City.

September 5th Governor’s Debate at the South Dakota State Fair, Huron

September 12th Meet & Greet, Wakonda

I’m showing up, I’m listening, and

I’ve got your back.

I look forward to visiting again, and to keep this important dialogue happening. | | | | | | | | Economic Development Should Start at Home South Dakota needs an economic development strategy that invests in South Dakotans; not one that gives tens of millions of dollars to large, out-of-state companies while producing little economic benefit for our communities. We recently provided $69 million to an out-of-state company that resulted in a couple hundred jobs paying about $18 an hour. That is a massive public investment for jobs paying wages that are comparable to what an individual can earn working in fast food in Sioux Falls. Supporters of these deals often point to the property tax revenue they generate. But we should ask a basic question: What is the economic benefit we are actually receiving for that investment? We could invest in affordable housing, create jobs through construction, and generate the same or greater property tax revenue while addressing a critical need in our communities. Meanwhile, there are South Dakotans ready to build businesses right here at home. While visiting Dakota Hemp in Wakonda, I met a farmer who is growing industrial hemp and wants to build a $3 million dollar factory to manufacture hempcrete. Hempcrete can be used in home construction and could become an important part of our affordable housing solutions. I asked him where he planned to build his plant. His answer was Iowa. When I asked why, he told me there were no economic incentives available to help him build it in South Dakota. Think about that. For the same $69 million we invested in one out-of-state company, we could have supported 23 projects like his across South Dakota. His plant would employ 10 to 12 people earning $22 to $25 an hour, while creating a new market for a South Dakota agricultural product. And this kind of small-business development can happen in communities across our state. As governor, I want to change our approach to economic development. We need to make it easier for South Dakota entrepreneurs, farmers and small businesses to start, expand and create good-paying jobs right here in our communities. When we invest locally, more of that money stays locally. It supports local businesses, local workers, local farmers and local communities. Economic development shouldn't just be about landing the biggest company. It should be about creating the greatest benefit for the people of South Dakota. | | | | | | | | Here’s where you can find me next. | | August 30th Latino Community Meet and Greet at the Augustana Lutheran Church, Sioux Falls August 30th Brookings County Democrats Potluck Picnic, Brookings Activity Center September 1st Super Tuesday with the Pennington County Dems at The Hive, Rapid City. September 5th Governor’s Debate at the South Dakota State Fair, Huron September 12th Meet & Greet, Wakonda I’m showing up, I’m listening, and I’ve got your back. | | | | | | | View email in browser

body:
On Women's Equality Day, we're remembering what Dolly Parton did with her seat at the table. |
---
[](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/137990816/642605080/-870569556?sourceid=1059902&refcode=WUEFET89_20260826_Dolly_PLEXP&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9UU00vVFNNRUwvMS84NzA2OSIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICJjMzAyZjljYi1hNWExLWYxMTEtOWIzMy0wMDIyNDgyYTlmMWQiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=pk3_YgPkm5kMCatvPMYL-Lf3IjkFWbH4hRyOloDffy4=) Peter, Yesterday we lost Dolly Parton. Today is Women's Equality Day. It feels almost too fitting to be a coincidence. Dolly Parton came from the Smoky Mountains and built an extraordinary life on her own talent and her own terms, in an industry that rarely made room for women to do either. But what made her legacy so remarkable wasn't simply the power she built. It was what she did with it. She gave books to millions of children. She invested in her home state and created jobs for her neighbors. She put significant funding behind the COVID-19 vaccine. Again and again, Dolly used her seat at the table to make room for others. **[Dolly embodied what we believe about women in leadership: When women have a seat at the table, they can lift entire communities with them.](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/137990817/642605081/-870569556?sourceid=1059902&refcode=WUEFET89_20260826_Dolly_PLEXP&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9UU00vVFNNRUwvMS84NzA2OSIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICJjMzAyZjljYi1hNWExLWYxMTEtOWIzMy0wMDIyNDgyYTlmMWQiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=pk3_YgPkm5kMCatvPMYL-Lf3IjkFWbH4hRyOloDffy4=)** | [ELECT WOMEN](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/137990818/642605082/1425818251?sourceid=1059902&refcode=WUEFET89_20260826_Dolly_PLEXP&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9UU00vVFNNRUwvMS84NzA2OSIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICJjMzAyZjljYi1hNWExLWYxMTEtOWIzMy0wMDIyNDgyYTlmMWQiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=pk3_YgPkm5kMCatvPMYL-Lf3IjkFWbH4hRyOloDffy4=)

And on Women's Equality Day, that feels particularly worth remembering. The 19th Amendment was a milestone, not a finish line. Women remain underrepresented at every level of government — and across much of the South, Democratic pro-choice women still face especially steep barriers to winning office.
That makes Dolly's story as a daughter of Appalachia especially powerful. She came from a region where the path to power for women has never been easy, reached extraordinary heights, and spent a lifetime using that power to empower others.

clean_body: On Women's Equality Day, we're remembering what Dolly Parton did with her seat at the table. | = Peter, Yesterday we lost Dolly Parton. Today is Women's Equality Day. It feels almost too fitting to be a coincidence. Dolly Parton came from the Smoky Mountains and built an extraordinary life on her own talent and her own terms, in an industry that rarely made room for women to do either. But what made her legacy so remarkable wasn't simply the power she built. It was what she did with it. She gave books to millions of children. She invested in her home state and created jobs for her neighbors. She put significant funding behind the COVID-19 vaccine. Again and again, Dolly used her seat at the table to make room for others. = | = And on Women's Equality Day, that feels particularly worth remembering. The 19th Amendment was a milestone, not a finish line. Women remain underrepresented at every level of government — and across much of the South, Democratic pro-choice women still face especially steep barriers to winning office. That makes Dolly's story as a daughter of Appalachia especially powerful. She came from a region where the path to power for women has never been easy, reached extraordinary heights, and spent a lifetime using that power to empower others. Across the South today, EMILYs List is working to make sure more women have the chance to do the same. That's why, this cycle, we’re proud to endorse dozens of women candidates across eight southern states. = If you've saved your payment information with ActBlue, your donation will go through immediately: = | = ---|--- = | = = | = Today, and every day, let's carry Dolly’s spirit forward. [](https://substack.com/redirect/c34575c1-a66a-40cf-b990-61a398435ca1?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Picture this.
You spend years inside one of the most powerful companies on Earth. You're an engineer. You're working on safety, the systems designed to protect people, including kids, from being exploited on the platform. You believe in the work. You give the company the benefit of the doubt.
Then you see them refuse to do right by it.
You bring the data to Mark Zuckerberg himself. Dozens of times. You sit across from him, show him what his platform is doing to children, and watch him take it in and do nothing.
Then on August 19th, you find yourself in a federal courtroom in Oakland. Forty-eight state attorneys general are in that room. The country is watching. You have one choice: tell what you know, or play it safe.
Arturo Bejar told what he knew.
He testified that the culture Zuckerberg has built at Meta makes it "practically impossible" to put proper child safety measures in place. Not difficult. Not a matter of funding. Practically impossible. And the only person with the power to change that, Zuckerberg... simply wouldn't.
So he called him a liar. By name. Under oath.
I know what that moment costs.
I was in the Capitol on January 6th. I was there in my uniform, holding the line, watching officers around me take blows from people who had been told by the President of the United States that we were the enemy. I was called racial slurs by people I had been trained to protect. And when it was over, I had to decide whether to tell the truth in front of Congress knowing full well who I was up against and what they were capable of.
There's a calculation that happens in that moment. You know the reach of the people you're calling out. You know how long their memory is. You know the industry you work in, the relationships you've built, and what goes on the line when you walk into that room and speak.
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack..zw0gH7hNrW_-naZ7CWQYXPtFdstK3jMcOkPkRd52N3U?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget&utm_content=212926079)
Bejar knew all of it. He spent years working at Meta. He knew exactly how deep this negligence went.
He testified anyway.
I'll be direct about why this matters beyond the courtroom.
Zuckerberg wasn't on the dais at Trump's inauguration by accident. He is not a tech executive who wandered into politics. He is power, the device in your pocket, your kid's phone, the platform that reaches billions of people and he has shown time and again that engagement is worth more to him than what it does to the children on the other side of the screen.
That's not my opinion. That's the data Bejar held in his hands for eight years.
Meta eventually put $17 billion on the table to settle. Analysts will tell you that's pocket change for a company that size. Forty-eight states put in years of work and the company wrote a check.
But you can't unwrite testimony. A settlement ends a lawsuit. It doesn't un-call a man a liar in open court when the charge is true and it's on the record.
That's what Bejar did.
There's nothing performative about it. It wasn't a press tour. It wasn't a book deal. It was a man who had been inside the machine, who knew exactly what it would cost him, and who chose to tell the truth anyway.
That's what we mean when we say good trouble.
Arturo Bejar -- Standing Our Ground Good Trouble honoree, August 26, 2026.
You tried to make it work from the inside for eight years. When you couldn't, you didn't go quiet. You went before 48 attorneys general and every parent in America and you told them the truth.
We see what that took. Thank you for it.

clean_body: This week's Good Trouble honoree is Arturo Bejar. | | ---|---|--- | | | Forwarded this email? ? for more This week's Good Trouble honoree is Arturo Bejar. | | | Aug 26 | | | | | | | | | | | | Picture this. You spend years inside one of the most powerful companies on Earth. You're an engineer. You're working on safety, the systems designed to protect people, including kids, from being exploited on the platform. You believe in the work. You give the company the benefit of the doubt. Then you see them refuse to do right by it. You bring the data to Mark Zuckerberg himself. Dozens of times. You sit across from him, show him what his platform is doing to children, and watch him take it in and do nothing. Then on August 19th, you find yourself in a federal courtroom in Oakland. Forty-eight state attorneys general are in that room. The country is watching. You have one choice: tell what you know, or play it safe. Arturo Bejar told what he knew. He testified that the culture Zuckerberg has built at Meta makes it "practically impossible" to put proper child safety measures in place. Not difficult. Not a matter of funding. Practically impossible. And the only person with the power to change that, Zuckerberg... simply wouldn't. So he called him a liar. By name. Under oath. I know what that moment costs. I was in the Capitol on January 6th. I was there in my uniform, holding the line, watching officers around me take blows from people who had been told by the President of the United States that we were the enemy. I was called racial slurs by people I had been trained to protect. And when it was over, I had to decide whether to tell the truth in front of Congress knowing full well who I was up against and what they were capable of. There's a calculation that happens in that moment. You know the reach of the people you're calling out. You know how long their memory is. You know the industry you work in, the relationships you've built, and what goes on the line when you walk into that room and speak. Bejar knew all of it. He spent years working at Meta. He knew exactly how deep this negligence went. He testified anyway. I'll be direct about why this matters beyond the courtroom. Zuckerberg wasn't on the dais at Trump's inauguration by accident. He is not a tech executive who wandered into politics. He is power, the device in your pocket, your kid's phone, the platform that reaches billions of people and he has shown time and again that engagement is worth more to him than what it does to the children on the other side of the screen. That's not my opinion. That's the data Bejar held in his hands for eight years. Meta eventually put $17 billion on the table to settle. Analysts will tell you that's pocket change for a company that size. Forty-eight states put in years of work and the company wrote a check. But you can't unwrite testimony. A settlement ends a lawsuit. It doesn't un-call a man a liar in open court when the charge is true and it's on the record. That's what Bejar did. There's nothing performative about it. It wasn't a press tour. It wasn't a book deal. It was a man who had been inside the machine, who knew exactly what it would cost him, and who chose to tell the truth anyway. That's what we mean when we say good trouble. Arturo Bejar -- Standing Our Ground Good Trouble honoree, August 26, 2026. You tried to make it work from the inside for eight years. When you couldn't, you didn't go quiet. You went before 48 attorneys general and every parent in America and you told them the truth. We see what that took. Thank you for it. * Standing Our Ground exists to put a face on the people who do the right thing when it isn 't safe or easy. If that matters to you, consider becoming a . subject: Will you hear me out?
body:
This is shaping up to be the toughest race of my life.
|

Please, Peter – just hear me out.
I’ve served as a two-term Democratic Governor in a swing state, so I know how to win tough races. I know how to expand Medicaid and pass paid parental leave for hundreds of thousands of people. I know how to fight back against an administration hell-bent on taking away our rights.
_What I don’t know?_ **How I’m going to win this race without folks like _you._**
Republican dark-money super PACs are spending nearly $100 million so far to attack my character and distort my record in front of millions of North Carolinian voters. **The attacks are false but they are working, Peter.** The latest poll has me _statistically tied_ with my Trump-backed opponent.
